summary: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation

summary: SylEmotions is a corpus of 7,051 Sylheti sentences labelled with seven emotions: Angry (1,000), Happy (1,001), Sad (1,000), Hate (1,004), Fear (999), Surprise (1,023) and Neutral (1,024). Each sentence is given in both Syloti Nagri and Bangla script. The file has three columns: syloti_in_bangla_script, syloti and emotion. Exact duplicates were removed. This dataset accompanies the paper "SylEmotions: A Dual-Script Corpus and Benchmark for Emotion Detection in Low-Resource Sylheti", 29th International Conference on Computer and Information Technology (ICCIT 2026).

summary: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models

summary: Can artificial intelligence reproduce the economic dynamics that emerge as households, firms and governments interact and adapt through markets and institutions? To answer this question, we define an economic world model (EWM) as an agent's internal representation of how an economic system works, enabling counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. We then propose a general framework for studying EWMs that links three tasks: simulating agent behaviour, learning economic transitions and systematically evaluating the dynamics. As an initial implementation, we learn household policies from microeconomic data and calibrate a structural economic transition model using macroeconomic data, linking individual decisions to aggregate dynamics. Our micro-to-macro evaluation framework compares simulated individual actions and group distributions with observed microdata and assesses macroeconomic dynamics through forecasting and counterfactual experiments. Results show that simulated and observed household consumption distributions overlap by 94.9%, while EWM forecasts closely track real GDP and several other aggregate levels. In government-borrowing counterfactuals, the EWM reproduces the benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission from borrowing to consumption. For ex ante planning, the EWM enables an LLM agent to achieve 10.29% higher simulated GDP under the epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions. This initial EWM is only a starting point. We invite economists and AI researchers to build a stronger EWM together. Economists can contribute richer economic models and knowledge, while AI researchers can develop stronger data-driven methods for simulating agent behaviour and learning economic transitions. Together, we aim not only to reproduce real economic dynamics, but also to discover and test new mechanisms that support better decisions and benefit society.

summary: The variational quantum algorithm ADAPT-VQE has previously been used to prepare the vacuum of lattice gauge theories in $1+1D$. In this paper, we study whether it extends to higher dimensions. We identify two general limitations of ADAPT-VQE. First, if the qubit Hamiltonian and the initial state are real, i.e., invariant under qubit-level time-reversal, all real-valued pool operators have vanishing gradients and are never selected. Second, the algorithm can converge to excited eigenstates. We illustrate both limitations, also providing examples from literature, and present a first application of ADAPT-VQE to a lattice field theory in $2+1D$, namely free Wilson fermions, where both obstacles occur. Adding charge conjugation symmetry to the operator pool improves the results, and combining different pools with suitable initial states recovers the ground and first excited states over the full mass range. These findings give practical guidelines for applying ADAPT-VQE to lattice field theories beyond $1+1D$.
title: Prospects and limitations of adaptive variational quantum algorithms for lattice field theories: a case study in 2+1 dimensions

summary: Spatial transcriptomics preserves the location of each expression profile, making it possible to study how gene regulatory networks differ within a tissue. Across regions of a tissue, regulatory relationships may vary and even reverse direction, so identifying the causal relationships in a specific pathological region can provide insight into therapeutic targets. We propose SpaDAG, a Bayesian method for learning spatially varying causal directed acyclic graphs. By defining the graphs on a triangulation of the tissue, SpaDAG allows each edge to have its own spatial pattern and even to reverse direction across regions. We show that the graphs nonetheless remain fully identifiable, and develop an MCMC sampler that explores them efficiently by reversing an edge over an entire connected region in a single move. SpaDAG outperforms competing methods in simulations with and without direction reversals. In a section spanning a renal cell carcinoma and the adjacent kidney, SpaDAG finds largely different relationships in the two tissues, with those in the tumor concentrated on genes associated with therapeutic targets. Between two of these genes, it identifies a relationship whose direction reverses across the tumor boundary, generating hypotheses about their region-specific coupling. Supplementary materials and code for this article are available online.
title: Bayesian Learning of Spatially Heterogeneous Causal Structure in Spatial Transcriptomics

summary: The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is proven to control the false discovery rate under independence and under positive dependence. Under arbitrary dependence, however, its guarantee deteriorates by a factor that grows logarithmically with the number of hypotheses. For Gaussian test statistics, it is unknown whether dependence can make the false discovery rate grow with the number of tests. We study this question when the correlation between two test statistics decays with the distance between their indices. We seek guarantees that hold uniformly over a wide class of correlation structures and over all configurations of the signals. We show that if the correlations decay at least as fast as a power of the inverse logarithm of the distance with exponent larger than one, then the false discovery rate of the original BH procedure is bounded by the nominal level times a factor that does not depend on the number of hypotheses. This factor grows only polylogarithmically as the level decreases. The result holds for both one- and two-sided tests, and the procedure uses no knowledge of the correlations. The class allows correlations of both signs. The required decay can be arbitrarily close to the inverse logarithm. The key technical tool is a truncated Hermite expansion of the exceedance indicators. It shows that their main fluctuations are common to all thresholds that BH may use. These fluctuations can be well controlled, while the remainder is too small to accumulate, which leads to a bound that does not inflate with the dimension.
title: A Dimension-Free Bound on the FDR of the Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure under Slowly Decaying Gaussian Correlations

This factor grows only polylogarithmically as the level decreases. The result holds for both one- and two-sided tests, and the procedure uses no knowledge of the correlations. The class allows correlations of both signs. The required decay can be arbitrarily close to the inverse logarithm. The key technical tool is a truncated Hermite expansion of the exceedance indicators. It shows that their main fluctuations are common to all thresholds that BH may use. summary: Directed transport in active matter is typically achieved by introducing geometric asymmetry, such as ratchets or gears, that rectify the stochastic motion of active particles. Here we demonstrate a fundamentally different route in which persistent mechanical motion emerges without any geometric bias. A symmetric passive rotor placed at the center of a circular domain undergoes spontaneous unidirectional rotation driven solely by the hydrodynamic flow generated by a boundary-confined flocks of Marangoni swimmers, despite the absence of direct physical contact. While individual swimmers produce intermittent torque reversals arising from transient hydrodynamic backflow, increasing the size of the flock establishes coherent circulation that stabilizes the rotor dynamics. Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reveals that the collectively generated flow transmits momentum over macroscopic distances, converting local active forcing into robust mechanical transport. Together with a minimal flow superposition model, our results identify the suppression of reverse-torque events as a collective signature of hydrodynamic coupling between active swimmers and a passive body, providing a contact-free mechanism for remote mechanical actuation in active matter.

summary: Independently pretrained vision and language models may learn shared structures of the same underlying world, providing a foundation for combining them to build multimodal capabilities. However, a key challenge remains in aligning cross-modal feature representations while preserving access to visual information before and after language adaptation. To this end, we propose sparse alignment with visual evidence-guided residual adaptation (SAVERA), a framework that combines frozen vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space and prompt-guided residual fusion. Specifically, we first present shared-space projection, activation reconstruction and encoding (SPARE), which represents original visual, adapted visual, and textual features through shared soft-gated sparse encoding, with branch-specific reconstruction to preserve their respective information. Second, we devise bridge--text embedding and activation matching (BEAM), a bidirectional cross-modal alignment module that aligns adapted visual and textual features at both the sample and neuron levels, establishing fine-grained cross-modal correspondence. Finally, we introduce prompt-conditioned residual integration of vision and adapted features (PRIVA), a prompt-guided residual fusion module that models vision--language interactions through gating and attention and integrates complementary information from original and adapted representations through residual fusion. Extensive experiments show that SAVERA achieves competitive performance on image captioning and visual question answering while reducing object hallucination.
title: SAVERA: Bridging Frozen Vision and Language Models via Sparse Alignment and Visual Evidence Reuse

summary: Lithography is a critical step in the manufacturing of chips that works by projecting light through a patterned mask and subsequently focusing it onto a photosensitive layer on top of a wafer. The task of finding a mask that prints a desired pattern on the wafer is called inverse lithography technology (ILT). The design of the mask is complicated by the fact that it must satisfy a set of constraints in order to be manufacturable. In this paper we provide a mathematical characterization of these constraints. Next, we develop a scoring function that allows us to measure whether a given mask satisfies the manufacturing constraints and if not, how badly the constraints are violated. Since our scoring function is (sub-)differentiable it can be used as the regularizer in a gradient-based inverse problem solver. We show that the resulting MorphILT algorithm that we developed can generate manufacturable masks that have nearly the same print quality as the (unmanufacturable) masks obtained from unconstrained inverse lithography.
title: A Morphological Approach to Inverse Lithography

We show that the resulting MorphILT algorithm that we developed can generate manufacturable masks that have nearly the same print quality as the (unmanufacturable) masks obtained from unconstrained inverse lithography.
title: A Morphological Approach to Inverse Lithography

summary: Maps are widely used in the robotics community for localization and path planning and the ability to identify incorrect or inaccurate regions of a map is an area of active research interest. For large environments, manual edits of the map can be very time consuming and a tool which can assist a map editor is needed. With this paper, we contribute to robot introspection through self-assessment of map quality, using only a given map as input to be independent of the underlying mapping algorithm. Current methods for map quality assessment rely on ground-truth or labelled information for training classifiers, both of which can be difficult to obtain. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised learning approach to map quality assessment of 2D occupancy grid maps which identifies regions of a map that require further investigation. We leverage an autoencoder for patches extracted from the map to capture the dominant structure of the map. By evaluating the reconstruction loss of a patch reconstructed with the learned model, we can evaluate whether it contains an unusual structure, which indicates the need of further investigation. We evaluate our method on the outcome of state-of-the-art grid mapping methods using benchmark datasets as well as maps from warehouse environments, highlighting the application to more complex environments. We show that the method identifies regions with sparse data, clutter, and misregistrations.
title: Self-supervised quality evaluation of grid maps without ground truth

summary: Pansharpening aims to fuse a single observed image pair, comprising a low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image and a panchromatic (PAN) image, to obtain a high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) image. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance due to their strong capability of extracting nonlinear features. However, distribution shifts between training data and test images can degrade the performance of pretrained pansharpening networks, limiting their generalization in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework that uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair to select and update only a subset of the pretrained network's parameters. Specifically, the framework uses cross-scoring to identify parameter groups whose updates improve reconstruction across image patches. It then updates the selected groups by minimizing a loss that combines a spectral consistency term with a newly designed spatial consistency term. Experiments show that the adapted networks perform better than their pretrained counterparts and outperform representative state-of-the-art pansharpening methods on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView series datasets.
title: Which Parameters to Update? An Instance-Specific Adaptation Framework for Real-World Pansharpening

summary: This maintenance release fixes issues in the Python package while keeping the interactive guide and existing analysis interfaces. Spectral analysis . Corrects odd-length FFT frequency labels and restores complex coefficient output with NumPy 2. FFT randomisation applies the same preprocessing settings to the observed and shuffled inputs. Fixes short-record Welch settings, aligns the settings used in paired spectra and corrects several significance thresholds. Wave analysis. Corrects k–ω Fourier bin alignment and radial power averaging while retaining the original smooth filter weights on the corrected grid. Fixes wavelet reconstruction scaling, POD mode accounting and SPOD filtering. EMD and EEMD honour requested preprocessing or ensemble settings. Installation. Repairs the command-line entry point, includes the licence and notices in the distributions, and lets pip select dependencies for Python 3.11 or later. Affected results can differ where a calculation was corrected. Historical FFT power scaling and the interactive quickstart are retained. See the installation guide or report an issue on GitHub .

summary: Versioned analysis-code and statistical-upgrade archive ( v3 , 24 November 2026) supporting Antagonistic pleiotropy at CTRB1/CTRB2 and shared polygenic architecture across pancreatic cancer, pancreatitis, and type 2 diabetes . Supersedes published v2 ( 10.5281/zenodo.24458358 ) and v1 ( 10.5281/zenodo.24339916 ) under Zenodo concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24339915 . New in v3: Upgraded 65-sheet supplementary workbook ( Additional_file_2_Tables_integrated.xlsx ; 55 cleaned original tables bit-for-bit preserved plus new tables S16–S25). Disjoint two-split cross-cohort MR meta-analysis, formal Fisher- z Steiger selection-bias audit, FinnGen R13 histology-restricted ductal PDAC leave- CTRB1/CTRB2 -out MR sensitivity, and locus-stratified CTRB1/CTRB2 and ABO pleiotropy decompositions (S16–S18). LDSC cross-trait intercept co-coding inversion and harmonized-scale Wray–Lee–Kendler (2012) liability-threshold misclassification grids for both PC–CP co-coding and pancreatogenic T3cDM/paraneoplastic NOD misclassified as T2D (S19–S20). Well-calibrated single-cohort UK Biobank–only T2D LDSC validation (univariate intercept 1.0630; S21). Full-R12 genome-wide PLACO pleiotropy scan (9.22–9.32M SNVs/pair) uncovering concordant NR5A2 (1q32.1) and pervasive antagonistic pleiotropy in metabolic–exocrine pairs, audited with both direct UK Biobank–only T2D PLACO and double-penalized fixed-variance genomic-control stress tests (S22). CAUSE v1.2.0 (4 disjoint splits with Pareto- k diagnostics), HM3 LCV, 72-model SuSiE-RSS ( 1000G_EUR_503 LD–Z mismatch audit), fitted .rds model objects, and East Asian LDSC (Yuan 2026 × BioBank Japan) power audit (S23–S25). Deterministic publication-grade SVG/PDF/PNG generators for Figures 1, 2c, 3, and 5. Original analysis code and documentation are released under the MIT License. All local workstation paths and non-public metadata have been scrubbed and verified against the root MANIFEST_SHA256.tsv . Archive scope: This release contains analysis code, selected derived results, the supplementary workbook, and 76 fitted model objects (72 SuSiE-RSS and 4 CAUSE). It is not a complete raw-data or historical MR/MAGMA-input mirror. Some reconstruction scripts require external GWAS/LD resources or the historical input bundles referenced in analysis_snapshot/README.md . Third-party resources retain their original terms.

summary: Conioscypha obovoideoispora L. Shao & J. Ma sp. nov. Fig. 3 Etymology. “ obovoideoispora ”, referring to the obovoid shape of the conidia. Holotype. GZAAS 23-0532 Description. Saprobic on unidentified decaying wood. Sexual morph: Undetermined. Asexual morph : Dematiaceous Hyphomycetous. Colonies on natural substrate effuse, black, gregarious, glistening. Mycelium semi-immersed, composed of hyaline to subhyaline, branched, septate, smooth hyphae. Conidiophores micronematous, mononematous, arising directly from the hyphae, and reduced to conidiogenous cells, hyaline. Conidiogenous cells phialidic, integrated, sessile or on micronematous conidiophores, with cup-shaped multi-collarette, hyaline, smooth. Conidia 12–18 µm × 12.5–18 µm (x ̄ = 15 × 14.4 µm, n = 30), acrogenous, solitary, globose to subglobose, obovoid, reddish brown to brown, aseptate, guttulate, smooth, truncate at base with a circular basal scar. Culture characteristics. Conidia germinating on PDA within 24 h, producing germ tubes from the basal cell. Colonies on PDA irregular to subcircular, dense, raised, fluffy, with undulate margins; surface velvety to finely floccose, distinctly zonate. Centre dark olivaceous-grey to greyish black, surrounded by a pale-yellow intermediate zone and a white to cream-white marginal fringe. Exudates and diffusible pigments absent. Reverse pale yellow to yellowish cream, olivaceous-grey to black at the center, becoming paler towards the margin; margin cream-white, crenate to slightly lobate. Diffusible pigments absent. Material examined. Saprobic on unidentified decaying branches, Liupanshui City, Guizhou Province, China, 29 th March 2023, Lei Shao & Jian Ma, LS 158 (GZAAS 23-0532, holotype), ex-type living culture GZCC 23-0527; LS 126 (GZAAS 23-0533, paratype), living culture GZCC 23-0528. Note. Our phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 1) shows that the newly isolated strains cluster with Conioscypha hydei (GZCC 24-0284) with robust support (99 % ML / 0.99 BYPP). Morphologically, our collection differs from C. hydei by its smaller conidia (12–18 μm vs. up to 26 μm) that are obovoid and guttulate, contrasting with the globose to subglobose conidia of C. hydei (Xiao et al. 2025). Sequence comparisons between our collection and the ex-type strain of C. hydei revealed significant nucleotide differences: 2.1 % in ITS (11 / 535 bp), 0.25 % in LSU (2 / 803 bp), 1.1 % in SSU (11 / 980 bp), and 4.3 % in RPB 2 (45 / 1,040 bp), excluding gaps. Based on both morphological distinctions and multigene phylogenetic evidence, our collection represents a novel species, herein introduced as C. obovoideoispora following the recommendations of Chethana et al. (2021). The two strains obtained in this study (GZCC 23-0527 and GZCC 23-0528) are morphologically identical. Pairwise sequence alignment between these two strains revealed minimal intra-specific variations, including 1 % in ITS (6 / 579 bp), 0.26 % in LSU (2 / 778 bp), and 0.4 % in SSU (2 / 488 bp excluding gaps). Therefore, both strains are accommodated within the same species and described here as C. obovoideoispora .

summary: Block Plugin Engine (BPE) is a C++ execution framework for ROS 2 applications based on dynamically loaded processing blocks. It provides configurable periodic, event-driven and multi-threaded scheduling, concurrent blackboard communication and generic ROS 2 input/output boundaries. Its architecture is designed to support predictable execution and memory behaviour in real-time robotic applications.

summary: Overview This reproducibility package (Version 2.2) accompanies the manuscript entitled “Evaluating Conclusion Stability in SDG Classification: A Provenance-Aware Multi-Model Benchmark of Higher-Education Web Data.” The study extends the evaluation layer of a broader Enumeration-First Information Systems research framework developed for the acquisition and mapping of institutional digital artifacts to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Within this research context, Institutional Host Space (IHS) provides an operational abstraction of institutional web sources, while the present study focuses on the downstream evaluation of SDG classification outcomes. Research Objective The objective is to examine the sensitivity and stability of classifier conclusions under different benchmark constructions, reference-evidence policies, and inferential resampling units. The proposed Evaluation–Conclusion Stability Framework (ECSF) serves as an operational reporting and diagnostic framework that distinguishes five non-interchangeable components of scientific conclusions: model ranking, paired effect magnitude, interval-based inferential decisions, uncertainty precision, and reference-evidence sufficiency. Empirical Scope The study draws on a frozen archive of 20,098 digital artifacts collected from 51 Indonesian higher-education institutions. Four recovered classifier configurations are evaluated: M0: Rule-based SDG classification. M1: TF-IDF with Linear Support Vector Classification. M2: Multilingual sentence embeddings. M3: Multilingual DistilBERT. The evaluation uses two operational benchmarks (A0: 328 artifacts; A1: 400 artifacts), two reference-evidence policies (B0 and B1), and two resampling units (artifact-level and institution-cluster bootstrap). B0 retains insufficient evidence (NSE) as an explicit human-reference outcome and evaluates fixed-18 Macro-F1, whereas B1 excludes human-NSE records and evaluates fixed-17 Macro-F1. These policies define distinct evaluation estimands. Main Findings The descriptive model ranking remained unchanged across the four benchmark-policy states. However, four of twelve cross-benchmark pairwise contrast-shift confidence intervals excluded zero under the recorded exploratory procedure. summary: The web contains vast amounts of scattered quantitative evidence that is difficult to organize into comparable and verifiable structures. Yet its unstructured, sparse, and sometimes conflicting nature makes a systematic distillation costly and error-prone. Existing approaches force users to make a trade-off: search engines return document lists that require labor-intensive extraction and reconciliation, while generative AI systems produce fluent summaries that obscure data provenance, introduce reporting bias, and hide inconsistencies. We present DataRecycle, an interactive system that helps transform scattered web evidence into structured tables of comparable numerical facts. Given a user's query or statement, DataRecycle decomposes it into entities and attributes, retrieves candidate evidence, and organizes scattered, potentially conflicting records in a table-based evidence view. To address key challenges in automated data distillation (i.e., incomplete retrieval, untraceable generation, sparse data distribution, and multi-source inconsistency), DataRecycle adopts an ontology-guided, top-down data acquisition strategy, visualizes the recorded lineage from retrieved snippets to extracted values, and aligns heterogeneous data across dimensions such as time, definition, and scale. We evaluate DataRecycle through module-level experiments, a usage scenario, and a user study, showing that the system helps users organize numerical web evidence into provenance-linked tables and inspect uncertainty and conflicting sources.
title: DataRecycle: Trustworthy Distillation of Structured Data from Scattered Web Evidence

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: A multi-agent group-generation system, as operated here, spends test-time compute uniformly across tasks. That a single agent's own vote distribution can gate its test-time compute is already reported by CATTS; we ask the multi-agent question: whether the distribution of stated confidences and critiques across a group of role-specialised agents predicts how hard a task is, which would let the group's compute be allocated adaptively. Taking as testbed a five-agent orchestrator for Perturb-seq response prediction inspired by CellForge and operated via MassGen, we define four trace metrics — Agent Confidence Entropy (ACE), Critique Severity Dispersion (CSD), a convergence signal (ΔC), and a Winner Flip Rate (WFR) — and their composite, the Task Difficulty Index (TDI). We pre-register five hypotheses with criteria: attainable error on Adamson 2016 (CRISPR interference) and Norman 2019 (CRISPR activation), the Architect agent's backbone-choice entropy, the rank correlation of each TDI component with held-out error, and cross-dataset transfer of a calibrated TDI. The design is 41 held-out K562 tasks (21 Adamson, 15 Norman singletons, 5 Norman doublets) drawn deterministically, a trainer sweep of 27 records per task and three fixed-length agentic lifecycle runs per task, all in one process. The agents are large language models (LLMs) from a pinned roster of Anthropic Claude models (Haiku 4.5 for the four proposer roles, Sonnet 5.5 for the Validator) whose served model is recorded and asserted per call; a run with any rule-based fallback step is invalid. Every run records its git revision, resolved configuration, library versions, dataset SHA-256 digests, task plan and label contract. We find that four of the five pre-registered hypotheses are supported and the cross-dataset transfer hypothesis is not; every hypothesis could be evaluated. The trainer sweep reaches the pre-registered error on both screens, and the Architect's choice of backbone varies above the pre-registered entropy floor. Within each screen, the drop in the agents' confidence across rounds, and the composite that inherits it, rank tasks by held-out error. From the second round on, however, every agent's prompt carries the previous round's held-out error, so that drop is stated after an error has been shown. In an exploratory analysis, the mean confidence stated before any feedback does not rank tasks by error (ρ = 0.003 on Adamson and 0.214 on Norman, both intervals including zero). Read with the design and that analysis, the pre-registered pass is consistent with stated confidence falling further where a larger error was shown; it is not evidence that the group's confidence anticipates difficulty. The composite fitted on Adamson did not meet the pre-registered transfer criterion on Norman (ρ = 0.286 against a criterion of > 0.4). The point estimates for confidence entropy, an evenness index over the agents, run against the pre-registered direction in both screens; this is exploratory, and no claim is made. The preflight probe and recommender are specified but not evaluated. The values reported in the earlier release of this work are superseded in full; the defects behind each are listed in the appendix.
title: Does Multi-Agent Confidence Predict Task Difficulty, or Only React to It? A Pre-registered Test on Perturb-seq

Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The library that did not own its readers In the imagined city of Meridian, the librarian inherited three copies of an ancient atlas. One could be read on the eastern terminal, one on the western terminal, and one in the shelter beneath the school. When the reader software was retired, all three became unreadable on the same morning. There was no fire, no lost disk, and no malicious visitor. The collection had survived in a form that nobody could open. Letter to the future: A letter to a librarian not yet born Build a library whose continued operation does not depend upon loyalty to its first librarian. Give later caretakers the authority to replace the catalog, repair the software, correct the record, and create new routes through the collection. Keep the old record when its lawful preservation matters; keep the correction equally visible. In a faraway city, the most valuable inheritance might not be an indestructible monument. It might be a modest institution that knows how to repair itself without silencing its readers. An archive object is usable only when its bytes, format, provenance and rights survive together. A manifest is not itself a reconstruction, and geographically separated disks may share one decoder. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Este trabalho relata a experiência de desenvolvimento e implantação do RIF, sistema web de controle de refeições estudantis do Instituto Federal de Educação, Ciência e Tecnologia de Rondônia (IFRO) – Campus Porto Velho Calama. O sistema surgiu da necessidade do Departamento de Assistência ao Educando (DEPAE) de superar o gerenciamento baseado na importação recorrente de planilhas e de ampliar o acompanhamento da utilização das refeições. A aplicação foi construída de forma incremental, a partir de requisitos levantados junto ao DEPAE e ao restaurante institucional, com PHP, CodeIgniter 4, MySQL e arquitetura MVC, e integra o cadastro de estudantes e usuários, a solicitação, a análise e o agendamento das refeições, a confirmação por mensagem e o registro de retirada por QR Code. Entre 3 e 31 de agosto de 2026, o RIF registrou 18.882 refeições liberadas, das quais 13.337 foram confirmadas (70,63%) e 10.464 tiveram retirada registrada, além de 2.873 confirmações sem retirada e 86 inativações, envolvendo 80 estudantes que ignoraram as mensagens de confirmação. Os resultados indicam que o sistema fornece ao DEPAE indicadores e históricos para o acompanhamento do benefício. A experiência evidenciou, ainda, as dificuldades formativas da equipe e o impacto da mudança de requisitos, e apontou a necessidade de um manual de procedimentos para orientar os novos integrantes.
title: RIF: SISTEMA DE CONTROLE DE REFEIÇÕES ESTUDANTIS DO IFRO – CAMPUS PORTO VELHO CALAMA

summary: This release provides crystal structures, thermal-conductivity data, pretrained DANA-$\kappa$ models, and computational workflows for high-throughput discovery of low-conductivity materials. It includes DANA-$\kappa$ predictions for 1,953,259 structures from Materials Project and Crystoria, 4,724 GRACE-based thermal-conductivity results, and CIF files for the 1,712 GRACE records satisfying $0<\kappa_{\mathrm L}<2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The DFT dataset contains 60 completed calculations with corresponding relaxed structures, including 58 phases below $2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and 29 below $0.5~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The lowest DFT value is approximately $0.1826~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{CsKAu_2}$. Conductivity values refer to 300 K and represent the diagonal average of the population-plus-coherence lattice thermal-conductivity tensor, excluding electronic conductivity. Additional resources include second- and third-order DFT force constants and reference transport outputs for the 58 low-conductivity phases, three split-specific DANA-$\kappa$ checkpoints, and scripts for inference, physical-property filtering, computational-cost estimation, structural deduplication, GRACE calculations, and VASP validation. Structure provenance, calculation settings, and quality annotations accompany the data to support reproducible analysis and subsequent model development.

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) over long time horizons is computationally expensive using traditional numerical methods. While neural operators provide an efficient alternative, they suffer from the accumulation of approximation errors along the predicted trajectory, typically caused by the failure to capture fine-scale details. In this work, we design a Commutator Memory Neural Operator that identifies fine-scale dynamical details by commuting two operations and leverages these details to enhance the neural operator's capability in capturing fine-scale features over long time horizons. Specifically, we identify a performance gap between two operations: downsampling the high-resolution field before rollout prediction versus performing rollout prediction before downsampling. We observe that fine-scale dynamical details are often encoded in this gap. By commuting these two operations, the fine-scale details removed during downsampling can be captured. Furthermore, we employ a memory module to store these fine-scale features along the trajectory and retrieve them during rollout, generating spatially adaptive corrections that enhance long-horizon fidelity. Empirical results across five systems demonstrate that CoMNO improves prediction accuracy and long-horizon rollout stability.
title: CoMNO: Commutator Memory Neural Operators for Long-Horizon PDE Prediction

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.
title: From Memory Access to Evidence Sufficiency: Diagnosing and Addressing Demand--Evidence Misalignment

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.
title: ExpGuard: Guarding Long-Horizon LLM Agents against Corrupted Experience

summary: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement. Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.
title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes
