direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Speculo  is an open-source  persistent data structure  for managing  speculative context states  in  long-context LLM serving . The library treats speculative context slices as a  probability distribution  (a  superposition ) and provides seven persistent operations:  add_candidate ,  measure ,  error_correct ,  refresh ,  evict_stale ,  collapse_to , and  branch . Speculo is a  classical analogue  of quantum superposition — not a quantum computer — and a  persistent state  for the LLM context, not a streaming  KV cache . The book documents the design, the  Python reference implementation  (2,185 LOC, 71 tests passing in 2.5s), the verified  arXiv-cited  competing systems (SpeContext, PRR, LongSpec, Superposition Prompting, SpecPV), and the user-facing API. The book is  honest about what is and isn't contributed : novel data structure, not a novel speculation algorithm. Speculo is the  third book  in a three-book series on persistent data structures for LLM systems, alongside  The Persistent Rope  (KV cache, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23241292) and  Anduril (agent state, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23265187). The three books together cover every persistent state in an LLM system. Apache 2.0. Source at github.com/lordxmen2k/speculo-context-processing
title: Speculo: Superposition and Measurement for Long-Context LLMs

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
title: ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Mechanisms recur across the sciences: the equation for heat in a solid also describes molecular diffusion or a Brownian particle. A mechanism is rarely written in one equation; its operation, boundaries, parameters and closures are stated at different steps of a derivation, where methods that read text or fit formulas miss it. We built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, and show that mechanisms can be compiled from them and constructed by deterministic calculation. A constructor detaches, transfers, unfolds, composes and joins their parts across disciplines; where parts do not fit, the failure is an equation for the missing term. Constructions turn a threshold reactor into a memory that a weak signal writes, an oscillator into a switch through two changes that each fail alone, and a rhythm into the regulator of a chemical amount, each with conditions for an experimental test.
title: Constructing physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.
title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Sharing brain imaging data supports secondary analysis and reproducibility, but privacy risks and differing legal and governance requirements can make unrestricted release inappropriate. The PublicnEUro repository was developed to support discovery and reuse under diverse legal requirements. Here, PublicnEUro's governance, architecture, BIDS-based deposition and curation, metadata and identifier services as well as open and controlled retrieval workflows are described. We then assess the repository published datasets against FAIR subprinciples and the repository public information against TRUST principles. The FAIR assessment shows strong findability and public metadata accessibility. The TRUST assessment documents governance, stewardship, continuity provisions and technical safeguards. Together this demonstrates that PublicnEUro, by separating open discovery from governed data retrieval, supports FAIR-aligned and trustworthy reuse of sensitive brain imaging data without requiring unrestricted disclosure.
title: PublicnEUro: A FAIR and TRUSTworthy infrastructure for controlled access to human neuroimaging data

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Add up the distances between every pair of points in a tree-shaped network with n vertices: this is the Wiener index, introduced by Wiener in 1947 to predict boiling points of paraffins and now a standard measure of how spread out a network is. If the diameter d (the longest distance) is prescribed, every distance is at most d, so the total lies below d times the number of pairs. How far below the largest possible total must fall is settled here to second order. Context. Plesník determined the least sum of distances for given order and diameter and remarked that upper bounds seem much more difficult; the maximum has since been called Plesník's problem (Cambie; Knor, Škrekovski and Tepeh, Problem 28). For trees, the maximum M d (n) lies just below (d/2 − ε/4)n 2 , ε the parity of d. Exact maximisers were known for d ≤ 4 and d ≥ n − 3, with sharp expansions for d ≤ 6 by Mukwembi and Vetrík. Cambie (2020) showed that the shortfall has order (dn) 3/2 and placed its coefficient between √2/3 ≈ 0.4714 and 29/60 ≈ 0.4833, in iterated limits; his lower construction already used branches forking into two at geometrically spaced heights (ratio about 0.38), and his lemma that every leaf of a maximiser lies at full depth is used in the proofs here. Main results. (1) Whenever d → ∞ and d/n → 0, with no order of limits imposed, the shortfall is (κ + o(1))(dn) 3/2 with κ = √((175 − √7)/756) ≈ 0.47747. (2) For each fixed d ≥ 4, M d (n) = (r + ε/4)n 2 − 2√c h n 3/2 − (zr + β h )n + O d (√n), with rational constants computed from the effective resistance of small rooted trees and tabulated for h ≤ 8; for example M 8 (n) = 4n 2 − √70 n 3/2 − n + O(√n). (3) For large n every maximiser is built from a finite catalogue of branch shapes, so for each fixed d an exact algorithm running in time polynomial in log n exists. (4) An explicit formula for M 5 (n) and all its maximisers for every n ≥ 6. (5) Exact maxima for 6 ≤ d ≤ 11 and n ≤ 3000 locate where the catalogue takes over in the tested range. Method. An exact distance identity writes the shortfall as a sum over branches of a depth cost and the squared subtree sizes. Treating the leaves as an electric current from the centre, the squared sizes are the energy of the current, so each branch costs its depth cost times an effective resistance. For large diameter this becomes a continuum problem (mass flowing down, splitting for free), solved by the calibration V = τ 2 /2 + τx 2 − x 4 /7, whose splitting excess is a sum of two squares: equality only for equal binary splits at heights τ = x 2 /2, so the remaining height shrinks by the factor 1/4 at each split. Limits. Trees only: for odd d graphs beat the tree leading term, and for even d the constant answers Plesník's problem for graphs only if Cambie's question (are the graph maximisers trees for large n?) has a positive answer. The constant κ is the leading coefficient; lower-order terms in the joint regime are open, as is the regime d/n → ρ > 0. The thresholds of the fixed-diameter and shape theorems are effective but not computed, and the fast algorithm is proved to exist but is not implemented. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); nine Python scripts with their recorded outputs: the coefficient table, the diameter-five formula against exhaustive enumeration up to 19 vertices, an independent recursion and the order-249 example (M 8 (249) = 215016), the large-height constructions, an exact symbolic certificate of every Section 5 constant, a claims check and the exact maxima for diameters 6 to 11 up to 3000 vertices; the bibliography, a machine-readable index, a research-gate record, a review summary, a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Every check fails explicitly, also under python
title: The maximum Wiener index of trees with prescribed diameter: the sharp second-order constant

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.
title: Unjamming Deferrals: Supporting Students Through JAMN Bot, a Mobile RAG-Grounded Policy Assistant

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and distinguishing demonstrated interoperability from stronger conformance claims.
title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.
title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Multimodal protein language models unify sequence and discrete structural tokens via iterative masked decoding, offering a promising paradigm for joint protein design. However, standard decoders rely on a memoryless mask reset at each iteration: only a sparse subset of newly committed hard tokens is carried forward, while all remaining unresolved sites are reset to an identical [MASK] embedding. In open-ended co-generation where neither modality provides a fixed external anchor, this stateless transition limits single-step refinement depth and deprives both tracks of stable cross-step soft anchors, leading to slow convergence or degenerative repetitive collapse. Observing that uncommitted predictions evolve with pronounced temporal coherence rather than erratic noise, we introduce Predictive Memory (PredMem), a training-free self-conditioning recurrence that carries these soft beliefs across steps. At each step, PredMem summarizes raw logits into a probability-weighted Top-$k$ expectation embedding at every residue and affinely interpolates it into eligible masked inputs on the next step at zero extra denoiser cost. Across DPLM-2, DPLM-2.1, and ESM3, PredMem raises unconditional sequence-structure co-generation success by 3.6, 17.7, and 48.7 percentage points, respectively, while improving the quality-diversity trade-off and suppressing repetitive mode collapse. Controlled diagnostics show that these gains stem primarily from early trajectory stabilization in unanchored cross-modal co-evolution rather than extra compute or simple entropy reduction, establishing PredMem as an efficient inference mechanism for multimodal discrete generation.
title: Beyond Hard Tokens: Predictive Memory for Multimodal Protein Generation

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) enables energy-efficient language-model inference, but hardware non-idealities perturb matrix--vector multiplications and degrade generation quality. Autoregressive (AR) models are especially vulnerable: each token is committed to the causal context at birth, so perturbation-induced errors cascade. We study diffusion language models (DLMs), which iteratively refine a masked sequence, as an alternative paradigm. Across scale-matched model pairs and open checkpoints, DLMs degrade more gracefully than AR counterparts under persistent weight perturbations. Controlled analyses rule out cross-round noise averaging and support delayed token commitment and progressive context resolution as the mechanism. A larger denoising-step budget further shrinks the clean--noisy gap, a DLM-specific latency--robustness knob. We perform large-scale simulation tests across diverse datasets and models using a noise model calibrated from real silicon measurements. Furthermore, on a 16-chip 28nm eFlash AIMC cluster, hybrid on-board measurements show DLMs tolerate $1.4$--$3\times$ larger weight noise, making diffusion-based generation a promising paradigm for noise-resilient AIMC inference.
title: Beyond Autoregression: Diffusion Language Model is All Analog In-Memory Computing Need

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to relate past experience, current spatial state, and future motion while following natural-language instructions. Recent approaches improve these capabilities through long-horizon memory, state-aware reasoning, and future prediction, yet these components are often modeled separately, leaving navigation state evolution insufficiently connected across time. We argue that camera pose provides a natural geometric representation for bridging past, present, and future states. Based on this insight, we propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework that jointly learns navigation decisions and geometric state evolution. PoseVLN organizes visual memory and the current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame, and jointly predicts the next K navigation actions together with a local $Δ$Pose over the same horizon. The predicted $Δ$Pose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to obtain the future pose state, which is recursively propagated throughout navigation, forming a continuous geometric state evolution from past memory to future motion. Experiments on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling geometric state evolution, with PoseVLN outperforming the strongest compared baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate, respectively, using only single RGB observations.
title: PoseVLN: Learning Geometric State Evolution for Vision-Language Navigation

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Memory-augmented large language model (LLM) driving agents can reuse past experience, yet previously learned corrections often fail to transfer when traffic conditions change. A key limitation is that existing memories mainly record observed outcomes, providing little evidence about alternative actions. We introduce XMind, a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving to "Think Twice" through cross-memory reasoning. XMind integrates working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The agent first makes an initial decision from the current context and then cross-checks it against retrieved historical experience. If a conflict arises, it makes a second decision guided by the retrieved evidence. To construct reliable episodic memory, XMind evaluates alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and stores the verified outcomes as structured risk capsules. These capsules are retrieved by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics. Across closed-loop highway simulations, XMind achieves success rates of 83.3-93.3%, exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average. Evaluation on K-Risk further demonstrates lower decision risk on unseen real-world high-risk interactions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. Code is available at https://github.com/xiangxiangliuwo/XMind
title: XMind: Thinking Twice via Cross-Memory Reasoning for LLM-Based Autonomous Driving

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Multimodal retrieval must match dense pages, fine-grained entities, ordered video, and agent tools and memory. Single-vector embeddings lose local evidence, cross-encoders reread every recalled item online, and uncompressed late interaction is too large to serve. We present OmniEVIE, a 4.5B multi-vector embedding model covering text, images, visual documents, video, and tools with one compressed index and a three-stage retriever. Each record stores at most 128 int8 vectors of dimension 64 (9,472 bytes, or 8.82 GiB per million records), providing a mean vector, 1-bit signs, and int8 multi-vectors for coarse, middle, and final search while localizing each hit to a page region or video interval. Training, merging, indexing, and retrieval are co-designed: all tasks share one retrieval format, a three-grade evidence check removes false negatives, dynamic sampling follows the baseline-teacher gap, candidates are compressed with ST-HAC during training to match the index, stage-wise and specialist models are merged by parameter block, and a saliency gate with a noise floor refines query scoring. Trained on public datasets, OmniEVIE scores 60.68 (full d=2048 sequence) and 60.06 (K128 x d64 int8 index) on MMEB-V3 (190 tasks), 77.96 on MMEB-V2 (78 tasks), and 62.96 on ViDoRe V3 (48 tasks). On 1M and 5M records, a single-thread query takes 54.2 ms and 120.2 ms (11.1x and 25.3x faster than exact 4096-d single-vector search; 236x and 532x faster than full int8 MaxSim). Video is encoded directly from frames without a parsing model: on QVHighlights (1,083 queries), the peak falls inside the labeled segment for 78.0% of queries and the returned span (18% of video length) intersects it for 94.3% vs. 44.9% random. Weights and code: https://huggingface.co/tencent/OmniEVIE-4B and https://github.com/Tencent/OmniEVIE.
title: OmniEVIE: Evidence-Vector-Informed Embedding for Multi-modal Retrieval

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.
title: CoverMem: Coverage-Constrained Visual Memory for Budgeted Embodied Question Answering

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 < 0$). We present PhysRF-WorldJEPA, a manifold-decoupled Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) that separates continuous electromagnetic state prediction from cross-modal language alignment. An unattenuated 1.0x clock anchor and parallel dual-scale RF encoder feed a lean ~3% LoRA LLM trained with two-step state-space EMA-JEPA (Denoise -> Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.
title: PhysRF-WorldJEPA: Transforming Heterogeneous Large Language Models into Manifold-Decoupled Millimeter-Wave Radar World Models

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.
title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
title: Integral DeltaNet: Improved Linear Attention with Adaptive Memory Integration

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: The Parallel--Serial-with-Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem with Power Peak Minimization (PSCALB3PM) was introduced by Delorme and Gianessi (2022), who proposed an integer linear programming (ILP) model, and further developed in 2024 with a multi-start local-search matheuristic. This paper presents an exact approach based on Boolean satisfiability (SAT) that combines a compact encoding with incremental SAT solving. Specifically, it develops a compact encoding of task-to-workstation precedence constraints and an incremental SAT-based optimization procedure for power peak minimization. We evaluate the proposed method on 375 benchmark instances and compare it with both reference methods. SAT finds feasible solutions for all 375 instances and certifies optimality for 159, compared with 346 feasible solutions and 126 optimality certificates obtained by the ILP method. Relative to the reference matheuristic, SAT achieves lower power peaks on 130 instances, whereas the matheuristic obtains lower values on only four. These findings establish SAT as a competitive exact method for PSCALB3PM, achieving higher feasible-solution coverage and more optimality proofs than the reference ILP model, while generally outperforming the existing matheuristic in terms of solution quality.
title: SAT Solving for Power Peak Minimization in the Parallel--Serial--with--Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
title: Cheap Memory Costs Future Compute: Co-Designing Persistent KV and GPU Execution for Efficient Streaming Video Diffusion

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (RTD) is a sample-efficient objective for pre-training text encoders, and RTD-trained models such as DeBERTaV3 are strong on classification benchmarks. The same models, however, are known to be poor backbones for embedding tasks such as retrieval and semantic similarity: the binary "original vs. replaced" signal does not ask the final layer to retain the token identity and contextual content that dense representations rely on. We introduce ModernELECTRA, a pre-training recipe that keeps RTD as the main objective and adds a lightweight auxiliary task, boundary-window reconstruction. For every token, we sample a window of 3-12 tokens that strictly contains it and reconstruct the token's original identity only from the discriminator's hidden states at the two window boundaries. The task costs one small FFN at training time and is discarded afterwards, yet it forces every final-layer state to carry information about its neighbourhood. Combined with a frozen, separately pre-trained generator, a temperature curriculum for hard negatives and a 512-to-8192 length curriculum, we train two compact encoders: EdgeCoder-31M, an 8-layer English model, and EdgeCoder-Multilingual-61M, a 16-layer model covering 46 languages, each on about 1T tokens. They reach 86.0 and 85.1 on GLUE. The English model outperforms Ettin-Enc-32m (83.5) and MiniLM-L12 (84.6) on GLUE while matching them on MTEB English v2 (51.1), and the multilingual model outperforms the 2.3x larger mmBERT-small on GLUE and Multilingual MiniLM and mDistilBERT on XTREME over the languages it covers. We also describe FlashDeBERTa, our open-source fused implementation of DeBERTa's disentangled attention that stores no $n \times n$ score matrix: at 4096 tokens it is 10x faster and uses 93% less memory than the reference implementation, and it loads existing DeBERTa checkpoints unchanged.
title: ModernELECTRA: Replaced-Token Detection with Boundary-Window Reconstruction for Compact Encoders that Classify and Embed

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(DΦ) = 1) without topological folding (det(DΦ) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox). We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(Ω) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(Ω). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations). We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(DΦ)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.
title: Exact Volume-Preserving Diffeomorphic Shear Splitting: Continuous-Discrete Geometric Bounds, Reversible Memory Backpropagation, and Expressivity Frontiers in Volumetric Mapping

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.
title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.
title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.
title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.
title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.
title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.
title: Interactive Neural Computers

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: We propose NABLA, a noise-adaptive blockwise left-right preconditioning algorithm for mini-batch stochastic nonconvex optimization. NABLA combines an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients with block-diagonal row and column preconditioners constructed from matrix-valued second-moment statistics. Unlike conventional matrix-preconditioned methods that use fixed decay parameters, NABLA adjusts the second-moment averaging coefficient through a closed-loop feedback rule determined by the cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average. The first-moment coefficient remains fixed, allowing the trajectory-dependent adaptation to act directly on the structured preconditioners. The resulting method is horizon-free, requires no prior knowledge of the noise level, and automatically adjusts the memory of its second-moment estimators to the observed optimization dynamics. Under standard lower boundedness, smoothness, unbiasedness, bounded-variance, and spectral-boundedness assumptions, we establish uniform stability and variation bounds for the time-varying block preconditioners and control their interaction with momentum estimation and parameter updates. These results yield the noise-adaptive stationarity guarantee $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2}+σ^{1/2}T^{-1/4})$, which automatically reduces to the nearly deterministic $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ rate when the stochastic-gradient noise vanishes. NABLA therefore provides a principled approach to combining closed-loop trajectory feedback with memory-efficient structured matrix preconditioning.
title: NABLA: A Noise-Adaptive Blockwise Left-Right Preconditioning Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Knowledge-tracing benchmarks often compare models that have different access to a learner's previous responses. We examine how data provenance, history length, and representation affect those comparisons. First, we compare a pinned ASSISTments 2009 sequence mirror against the corrected official release. Of 4,148 learners represented in both, 817 have different ordered skill-response sequences; the mirror also contains fewer labeled events. Second, we retain earlier learner-disjoint model evaluations on the 2009 and 2015 datasets, distinguishing exploratory results from a corrective 2015 replication. Finally, we evaluate a new, nonoverlapping sample of 4,000 ASSISTments 2015 learners using three models constrained to the same one-event or 20-event prior-response window. On 20,592 test responses from 582 learners, the 20-event Brier scores were 0.17667 for count-based logistic regression, 0.17389 for an order-aware logistic model, and 0.17514 for a GRU. The GRU-minus-order-aware difference was 0.00125 (95% learner-cluster bootstrap interval [0.00008, 0.00243]); at one prior event, the corresponding difference was 0.00212 [0.00120, 0.00301]. Earlier comparisons had favored the GRU against simpler history summaries. The newer analysis instead favors a logistic comparator that represents order using the same permitted event stream. These results concern predictive performance on particular historical cohorts and model settings. They neither isolate an architectural effect nor establish generalization to contemporary classrooms.
title: When Knowledge-Tracing Rankings Depend on Available History: A Source-Correction and Matched-Information Audit on ASSISTments 2009 and 2015

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: The dataset is a canonical, machine-readable compilation of 756 relinquishment reports for production licences on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, submitted by licensees and made public by the Norwegian Offshore Directorate (Sodir). Each report is represented by one structured JSON record and one GeoJSON file of its mapped features. The records were produced by a large-language-model extraction of the report PDFs and cover licence history (licensees, work commitments, milestones and reasons for relinquishment), the prospects and leads evaluated in each licence (play, trap, reservoir, risk factors and geological chance of success, volume distributions per evaluation stage, and drilling results), and the seismic data and studies used. A reproducible pipeline harmonised these records into a single canonical schema without altering any source value: all 2,016,399 source values were retained verbatim at their original paths, which was verified for every record by rebuilding the source file from the canonical record and comparing the two value by value, including data types, number formats and array order. Computed values are kept strictly separate from source content: 203,570 normalised values are stored in dedicated  _derived  objects next to the value they describe, and each records the source fields it was derived from, the rule applied and a status (exact 198,437; approximate 1,346; suggested 500; requiring review 2,766; not normalisable, unclassified or ambiguous 521). Normalisation comprises: conversion to common units: oil and oil-equivalent volumes in 10⁶ Sm³, gas in 10⁹ Sm³, depths in metres and ratios as fractions, with barrel and boe conversions labelled approximate (1 Sm³ o.e. = 6.29 boe); evidence-based orientation of probabilistic volumes to the convention that P10 is the high estimate, applied to 4 distributions, while 15 internally inconsistent distributions were flagged rather than reordered; parsing of dates with explicit precision; standardisation of licence identifiers, well names, lithostratigraphic and chronostratigraphic names, trap types, AVO classes and study categories. Ambiguous cases are never resolved by assumption, because the mapping tables are versioned and only entries approved by a person are applied; in the current version, for example, 1,319 company-name variants and 420 meeting types remain listed for review. The spatial component comprises 7,162 features (prospect and lead outlines, licence boundaries, well locations and seismic survey outlines) in EPSG:4326 with geometry unchanged from the source; it is provided both as a combined layer and as one file per report, and its attributes are reduced to identity and link information so that the JSON records are the single source of truth for all descriptive attributes. Features are linked to their report entities through explicit identifiers (5,644 prospect links) or through name-based matching flagged for review (29 links, including 6 segment-to-parent relations), and the attributes previously duplicated in the GeoJSON files were compared against the records in 250,664 value-level checks whose discrepancies, such as systematic unit-scale differences in 48 reports, are published as quality-control reports rather than corrected. Provenance is kept at every level: each record and feature carries its source file name, SHA-256 fingerprint, pipeline, schema and mapping-table versions; the source files are archived byte for byte; and the extraction's own uncertainty markers are preserved, with 48,200 values marked as stated in the report, 3,057 as inferred by the extractor and 467 as read from figures, extractor confidence levels for 863 prospects, and 2,757 of 7,162 features marked for review. Because the canonical dataset is faithful to the extracted records but has not been verified against the original PDFs, it should be used together with its validation, unresolved-field and consistency reports, and quantitative values should
title: 756 Norwegian Oil and Gas License relinquishment reports with associated prospect leads and ideas extracted as canonical JSON files for consistent database entry

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Unit-level audit of dataset reuse across 30 osteoporosis drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) studies. The record contains the frozen analysis tables, the adjudication ledger and the code that produced the figures, tables and numbers of the accompanying manuscript. What was measured - 128-study frozen corpus (musculoskeletal drug-target MR); 55 studies concerned osteoporosis or bone mineral density; 30 entered at least one candidate comparison (a target nominated in two or more studies). - 133 dataset units (one study x one dataset): 103 study-level rows plus 30 units expanded from two composite rows; 110 usable (84 as extracted, 26 after correction), 23 rejected because the resource name was absent from the supporting sentence. - 22 dataset families. Exposure concentrated in eQTLGen (9 studies), the deCODE plasma proteome (9) and the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (6); FinnGen supplied the outcome in 13 studies. - 34 study pairs share an exposure family and an outcome family: 11 identical dataset, 8 same endpoint with release unstated, 6 same endpoint at different releases, 7 not adjudicable, 2 demonstrably different. 25 of 34 (73.5%) analysed the same outcome endpoint; 92.6% among the 27 pairs where both studies named the endpoint; 94.1% only if every non-adjudicable pair shared it. - Endpoint identity was recoverable for 12 of the 13 FinnGen-outcome studies. Files - data/S1_unit_table.csv - the 133 units with the supporting sentence, verdict and naming correction flag (Table S1). - data/S2_pair_grades.csv - the 34 pairs with their five-level grade (Table S2). - data/S3_family_matrix.csv - the 22 families with exposure/outcome study counts (Table S3). - data/S4_naming_corrections.csv - the 19 naming corrections applied before grading (Table S4). - data/source_evidence.csv - evidence sentences with the locator used for each recorded dataset. - data/finnengen_endpoint_counts.csv, data/release_ladder.csv - release-specific case and control counts used to recover endpoint identity. - data/dataset_audit_full.csv, data/pair_matrix.csv - the full audit table and the pair matrix before grading. - data/corpus_128_studies.csv, data/target_nominations.csv - the frozen corpus and the target nominations from which the 30 comparative studies were selected. - data/analysis_summary.json - retrieval counts (4,446 records, 2,759 after de-duplication, 262 at screening). - data/references.csv - the reference table with PubMed identifiers. - code/ - the scripts that build the registries, the pair grades, the figures, the manuscript and the two self-checks (number registry; citation numbering). - docs/ - project.json (design type, frozen state, positive control), numbers.json (every number in the manuscript with its source), claim-ledger.tsv, figures.tsv. Provenance The corpus was assembled on 16 November 2026 by seven search batches over Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Crossref (Semantic Scholar could not be queried because of rate limiting) and frozen before any dataset-level extraction. 4,446 records were reduced to 2,759 after de-duplication and to 262 at title-and-abstract screening; 128 publications formed the main set. How to re-run Python 3.11; set F11_ROOT to the directory containing data/, code/ and docs/, then follow code/README_run_order.md. The two gates are lint of the manuscript (external tool) and code/145_refs45_align_numbered.py (citation numbering). Absolute paths and the local host name were replaced with environment variables in this deposit; no analysis input was altered. Licence Data and derived tables: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT. Status Manuscript in preparation; not yet submitted. No DOI for the article exists at the time of deposit.
title: Dataset reuse in osteoporosis drug-target Mendelian randomization: unit-level audit tables, adjudication ledger and analysis code

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
title: SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report

summary: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation

summary: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models

summary: Block Plugin Engine (BPE) is a C++ execution framework for ROS 2 applications based on dynamically loaded processing blocks. It provides configurable periodic, event-driven and multi-threaded scheduling, concurrent blackboard communication and generic ROS 2 input/output boundaries. Its architecture is designed to support predictable execution and memory behaviour in real-time robotic applications.
title: Block Plugin Engine (BPE)

summary: Overview This reproducibility package (Version 2.2) accompanies the manuscript entitled “Evaluating Conclusion Stability in SDG Classification: A Provenance-Aware Multi-Model Benchmark of Higher-Education Web Data.” The study extends the evaluation layer of a broader Enumeration-First Information Systems research framework developed for the acquisition and mapping of institutional digital artifacts to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Within this research context, Institutional Host Space (IHS) provides an operational abstraction of institutional web sources, while the present study focuses on the downstream evaluation of SDG classification outcomes. Research Objective The objective is to examine the sensitivity and stability of classifier conclusions under different benchmark constructions, reference-evidence policies, and inferential resampling units. The proposed Evaluation–Conclusion Stability Framework (ECSF) serves as an operational reporting and diagnostic framework that distinguishes five non-interchangeable components of scientific conclusions: model ranking, paired effect magnitude, interval-based inferential decisions, uncertainty precision, and reference-evidence sufficiency. Empirical Scope The study draws on a frozen archive of 20,098 digital artifacts collected from 51 Indonesian higher-education institutions. Four recovered classifier configurations are evaluated: M0: Rule-based SDG classification. M1: TF-IDF with Linear Support Vector Classification. M2: Multilingual sentence embeddings. M3: Multilingual DistilBERT. The evaluation uses two operational benchmarks (A0: 328 artifacts; A1: 400 artifacts), two reference-evidence policies (B0 and B1), and two resampling units (artifact-level and institution-cluster bootstrap). B0 retains insufficient evidence (NSE) as an explicit human-reference outcome and evaluates fixed-18 Macro-F1, whereas B1 excludes human-NSE records and evaluates fixed-17 Macro-F1. These policies define distinct evaluation estimands. Main Findings The descriptive model ranking remained unchanged across the four benchmark-policy states. However, four of twelve cross-benchmark pairwise contrast-shift confidence intervals excluded zero under the recorded exploratory procedure. Across 24 fixed-prediction comparisons, eleven institution-cluster bootstrap intervals were wider and thirteen were narrower than their artifact-level counterparts. Twenty-three comparisons produced concordant zero-exclusion decisions, while one comparison produced a discordant decision at an unchanged point estimate. The H400 reference ledger recorded agreement between two label columns for 393 of 400 artifacts, with adjudication documented for the remaining seven cases (Cohen's kappa = 0.977). These findings demonstrate that observed ranking stability does not necessarily imply stability across all components of classifier evaluation conclusions. Package Contents The package supports the reproducibility and auditability of the reported derived analyses through: Derived evaluation datasets and result tables. Frozen reference and prediction outputs. Analysis scripts and archived bootstrap result ledgers. De-identified reference-label traceability records. Benchmark and evidence-policy documentation. Scoped duplicate-sensitivity and lexical-retrieval audit results. Execution protocols and SHA-256 checksum manifests. README, data dictionary, citation metadata, and version history. Package integrity and reproducibility verification documentation. Version 2.2 aligns the package documentation and citation metadata with the accompanying manuscript while preserving the frozen empirical data, model outputs, analysis scripts, and reported experimental results. Reproducibility and Limitations The package supports derived evaluation and audit reproducibility, including the recalculation of selected evaluation metrics, verification of archived result ledgers, reference-label reconciliation, and integrity chec
title: Reproducibility Package for Evaluating Conclusion Stability in SDG Classification: A Provenance-Aware Multi-Model Benchmark of Higher-Education Web Data

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.
title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: See the README.md of the individual crates for their own changelogs. The crates are now grouped into core , language , rewriter and transition_systems directories. This release adds a native type checker for the mCRL2 specification language. The new merc_typecheck crate type checks data specifications, including overload resolution, implicit numeric coercions, structured sorts and the polymorphic system-defined containers. The syntax tree now carries span information, which gives precise error messages and is the basis for a language server. Parsing of deeply nested if-then-else expressions is no longer quadratic. The new merc_explore crate provides a generic explicit state space exploration framework, with optional caching of summand enumeration, a control flow graph analysis and parallel (work stealing) exploration. It is used by merc-lps explore-explicit , by the PBES exploration and by merc-lts combine . The latter now caches enabled actions and shares action labels, which makes it considerably faster. The merc_ldd crate has been removed in favour of the LDD implementation of OxiDD . Symbolic reachability in merc-symbolic now supports chaining and saturation (following Ciardo) and summand grouping. The merc-pbes tool has been extended considerably. It can now explore PBES explicitly or symbolically into parity games, and solve them ( solve , solve-symbolic ). The merc-rewrite tool can now parse full mCRL2 specifications and has a new check command to type check data specifications. merc-lts supports the binary LTS formats where sensible, no longer converts i to tau when reading AUT files, and requires an output for convert . The explicit parity games and LTSs use compressed vectors to reduce memory usage. The merc_aterm crate has been reviewed to ensure that safe code cannot lead to undefined behaviour. In particular, Protected containers are now written through a scoped closure. Terms and function symbols have a more compact layout, the term parser no longer depends on pest, and garbage collection marking uses pointer tagging instead of a hash set. Full Changelog : https://github.com/MERCorg/merc/compare/v2.0...main
title: MERCorg/merc: v3.0
