summary: Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.
title: AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction

summary: Robot-programming agents improve executable control policies through repeated testing and repair, yet binary success saturates while execution risk persists across unseen scenes. We introduce MARGIN, a risk-aware agent that converts successful robot rollouts into actionable evidence for program refinement. Its near-miss margin measures the fraction of the execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout. The agent uses this signal to prioritize fragile programs, guide targeted repairs, and select revisions that preserve development success while increasing execution headroom. An exact safe-racing rule accelerates success-based candidate evaluation. We evaluate MARGIN across LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-90, and Robosuite. In our 80-task LIBERO-Pro reproduction, 78 programs attain perfect development success while accounting for substantial failures on unseen seeds. The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774, and low-margin programs exhibit 2.97 times higher failure risk. Across two independent evaluation rounds spanning 37 unique LIBERO-Pro tasks, MARGIN reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0%, with reductions of 18.0-20.0% on LIBERO-90 and Robosuite. Safe racing reduces fixed-sequence candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% while retaining identical selections, and paired execution probes improve acceptance decisions by identifying hidden regressions. Together, these results establish near-miss evidence as an effective basis for risk-aware, budget-efficient robot program refinement.
title: MARGIN: A Risk-Aware Agent for Robot Program Refinement

summary: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.
title: From Memory Access to Evidence Sufficiency: Diagnosing and Addressing Demand--Evidence Misalignment

summary: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.
title: ExpGuard: Guarding Long-Horizon LLM Agents against Corrupted Experience

summary: This book is a  reproducible, grade-by-domain assessment of frontier AI capability in mid-2026.  Across  six reasoning domains  — math, code, planning, social reasoning, language, and scientific reasoning — the book assigns each domain a letter grade (A through F) and documents the  reproducible benchmark evidence  behind the grade. Every claim is anchored on  publicly available benchmarks  and on  models released on or before 2026-06-18 , the book's deliberate 4-month model-release cutoff. The grading system is  defensible, reproducible, and intentionally future-proof : it is designed to last longer than any specific benchmark or model.  The book is a snapshot of the mid-2026 frontier, not a verdict on AI's long-term trajectory. The book argues a single central claim:  frontier AI in 2026 is best understood as a very high-fidelity compression of the prior distribution of human problem-solving , with  selective generalization to nearby problems  but  reproducible failure on out-of-distribution, underspecified, or long-horizon tasks . The compression thesis is supported by three pieces of evidence: the  saturating benchmarks  (AIME 2026, LiveCodeBench, ARC-AGI-2) where frontier models now score at-or-above human level, the  emerging frontier benchmarks  (Riemann-Bench, CritPt, Senior SWE-Bench, Long-Horizon-TB, ARC-AGI-3) where the same models drop into the single digits, and the  CoT smoking gun  — the persistent gap between explicit Theory of Mind (near-perfect) and applied Theory of Mind (49.5% without CoT, jumping to 93.5% with CoT) on SimpleToM.  The book's contribution is the framework, the grades, and the evidence trail — not a verdict on whether the model is "intelligent" in any contested sense. The 4-month cutoff, the contamination audit, and the openly cited sources are the book's commitment to honesty.
title: The Grade Book: A Grade-by-Domain Assessment of Frontier AI Capability in 2026

summary: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.
title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics

summary: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and distinguishing demonstrated interoperability from stronger conformance claims.
title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training

summary: Memory-augmented large language model (LLM) driving agents can reuse past experience, yet previously learned corrections often fail to transfer when traffic conditions change. A key limitation is that existing memories mainly record observed outcomes, providing little evidence about alternative actions. We introduce XMind, a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving to "Think Twice" through cross-memory reasoning. XMind integrates working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The agent first makes an initial decision from the current context and then cross-checks it against retrieved historical experience. If a conflict arises, it makes a second decision guided by the retrieved evidence. To construct reliable episodic memory, XMind evaluates alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and stores the verified outcomes as structured risk capsules. These capsules are retrieved by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics. Across closed-loop highway simulations, XMind achieves success rates of 83.3-93.3%, exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average. Evaluation on K-Risk further demonstrates lower decision risk on unseen real-world high-risk interactions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. Code is available at https://github.com/xiangxiangliuwo/XMind
title: XMind: Thinking Twice via Cross-Memory Reasoning for LLM-Based Autonomous Driving

summary: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.
title: CoverMem: Coverage-Constrained Visual Memory for Budgeted Embodied Question Answering

summary: Latent world models learn compact recurrent dynamics from offline trajectories, yet deployed simulators can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions from outdated physical regimes. Existing unlearning methods fail in autoregressive physics: gradient updates distort latent manifolds and compound rollout drift, naive output zeroing suppresses valid control responses on trigger onset, and single-step deletion leaves corruption inside recurrent hidden states. We propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm for latent world models. Using only cached pretraining moments, ADE recovers retain covariances via single-pass matrix downdating without raw retain data and cascades closed-form edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states, and downstream heads. Pairing orthogonal excision with whitened recurrent damping and mean-preserving affine calibration neutralizes out-of-manifold backdoors and realigns in-manifold shifts without variance collapse. Across four regimes on three MuJoCo benchmarks, ADE outperforms seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1, eliminating HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers $4.4\times$ faster than fine-tuning, and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.
title: ADE: A Zero-Training Unlearning Method for Latent World Models

summary: The Parallel--Serial-with-Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem with Power Peak Minimization (PSCALB3PM) was introduced by Delorme and Gianessi (2022), who proposed an integer linear programming (ILP) model, and further developed in 2024 with a multi-start local-search matheuristic. This paper presents an exact approach based on Boolean satisfiability (SAT) that combines a compact encoding with incremental SAT solving. Specifically, it develops a compact encoding of task-to-workstation precedence constraints and an incremental SAT-based optimization procedure for power peak minimization. We evaluate the proposed method on 375 benchmark instances and compare it with both reference methods. SAT finds feasible solutions for all 375 instances and certifies optimality for 159, compared with 346 feasible solutions and 126 optimality certificates obtained by the ILP method. Relative to the reference matheuristic, SAT achieves lower power peaks on 130 instances, whereas the matheuristic obtains lower values on only four. These findings establish SAT as a competitive exact method for PSCALB3PM, achieving higher feasible-solution coverage and more optimality proofs than the reference ILP model, while generally outperforming the existing matheuristic in terms of solution quality.
title: SAT Solving for Power Peak Minimization in the Parallel--Serial--with--Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem

summary: Latent world models learn representations by predicting future states in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels. When training across multi-frame sequences, however, not all frames and spatial regions are equally informative or predictable. We argue that forcing a world model to minimize every prediction error may be unnecessary and harmful. Under standard $L_2$ loss, unbounded gradients force the encoder and predictor to overfit noisy or transient frames at the expense of core physical structure, while amplifying gradient conflict with representation regularizers. Conversely, $L_1$ loss bounds large gradients, but its constant gradient magnitude near zero disrupts the local smoothness required for planning. We resolve this tension with \textbf{ReJEPA}, a bounded predictive regulation principle that combines bounded gradients for large errors with smooth quadratic behavior near zero, instantiated simply via the element-wise $\log\cosh$ loss. As a drop-in training replacement across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA~2.1, $\log\cosh$ consistently outperforms $L_2$, a curvature-matched quadratic control, $L_1$, and Smooth-$L_1$ baselines without altering architectures or inference procedures. Notably, the gains grow with environmental complexity, scaling from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world autonomous driving on NAVSIM. Probing and geometric analyses confirm that relaxing the penalty on extreme errors yields representations that better capture physical states and align with the true planning cost landscape.
title: ReJEPA: Bounded Predictive Regulation for Latent World Models

summary: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
title: Cheap Memory Costs Future Compute: Co-Designing Persistent KV and GPU Execution for Efficient Streaming Video Diffusion

summary: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.
title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design

summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.
title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification

summary: Level 4 autonomous vehicles require fault-tolerant architectures that preserve critical driving functions under sensing, computing, communication, power, and actuation failures. As these systems progress toward industrial scalability, architectural complexity, validation burden, integration effort, and lifecycle cost become increasingly relevant. This study proposes an Operational Design Domain (ODD)-based, safety-constrained systems-engineering framework for architecture rationalization. ODD-specific capabilities, physical fault assumptions, post-fault operational policies, and spatial sensing requirements are propagated through an integrated safety-feasibility gate. Architecture transformations, including removal, relocation, functional reassignment, and consolidation, are evaluated only within the resulting safety-feasible design space, followed by lifecycle-cost sensitivity and robust multiobjective Pareto analysis. A generic, synthetically parameterized Level 4 architecture is used as a demonstrative computational case study. Within this modeled design space, direct ablation showed limited rationalization potential, whereas directional redistribution and functional consolidation generated a broader set of safety-feasible candidates. Under the illustrative lifecycle-cost model, the best nominal candidate achieved a 5.55% normalized cost reduction and remained cost-reducing across all 5,000 sampled points in the prescribed uncertainty domain. The analysis identified 15 non-dominated architecture-policy solutions representing seven physical transformations. The results support capability-based, policy-conditioned, and lifecycle-aware architecture rationalization under the stated assumptions, with safety retained as a non-compensatory feasibility constraint. The reported transformations are design candidates rather than validated production architectures.
title: From Safety-Driven Redundancy to Value-Driven Architecture: An ODD-Based Rationalization Framework for Level 4 Autonomous Vehicles

summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.
title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence

summary: The dataset is a canonical, machine-readable compilation of 756 relinquishment reports for production licences on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, submitted by licensees and made public by the Norwegian Offshore Directorate (Sodir). Each report is represented by one structured JSON record and one GeoJSON file of its mapped features. The records were produced by a large-language-model extraction of the report PDFs and cover licence history (licensees, work commitments, milestones and reasons for relinquishment), the prospects and leads evaluated in each licence (play, trap, reservoir, risk factors and geological chance of success, volume distributions per evaluation stage, and drilling results), and the seismic data and studies used. A reproducible pipeline harmonised these records into a single canonical schema without altering any source value: all 2,016,399 source values were retained verbatim at their original paths, which was verified for every record by rebuilding the source file from the canonical record and comparing the two value by value, including data types, number formats and array order. Computed values are kept strictly separate from source content: 203,570 normalised values are stored in dedicated  _derived  objects next to the value they describe, and each records the source fields it was derived from, the rule applied and a status (exact 198,437; approximate 1,346; suggested 500; requiring review 2,766; not normalisable, unclassified or ambiguous 521). Normalisation comprises: conversion to common units: oil and oil-equivalent volumes in 10⁶ Sm³, gas in 10⁹ Sm³, depths in metres and ratios as fractions, with barrel and boe conversions labelled approximate (1 Sm³ o.e. = 6.29 boe); evidence-based orientation of probabilistic volumes to the convention that P10 is the high estimate, applied to 4 distributions, while 15 internally inconsistent distributions were flagged rather than reordered; parsing of dates with explicit precision; standardisation of licence identifiers, well names, lithostratigraphic and chronostratigraphic names, trap types, AVO classes and study categories. Ambiguous cases are never resolved by assumption, because the mapping tables are versioned and only entries approved by a person are applied; in the current version, for example, 1,319 company-name variants and 420 meeting types remain listed for review. The spatial component comprises 7,162 features (prospect and lead outlines, licence boundaries, well locations and seismic survey outlines) in EPSG:4326 with geometry unchanged from the source; it is provided both as a combined layer and as one file per report, and its attributes are reduced to identity and link information so that the JSON records are the single source of truth for all descriptive attributes. Features are linked to their report entities through explicit identifiers (5,644 prospect links) or through name-based matching flagged for review (29 links, including 6 segment-to-parent relations), and the attributes previously duplicated in the GeoJSON files were compared against the records in 250,664 value-level checks whose discrepancies, such as systematic unit-scale differences in 48 reports, are published as quality-control reports rather than corrected. Provenance is kept at every level: each record and feature carries its source file name, SHA-256 fingerprint, pipeline, schema and mapping-table versions; the source files are archived byte for byte; and the extraction's own uncertainty markers are preserved, with 48,200 values marked as stated in the report, 3,057 as inferred by the extractor and 467 as read from figures, extractor confidence levels for 863 prospects, and 2,757 of 7,162 features marked for review. Because the canonical dataset is faithful to the extracted records but has not been verified against the original PDFs, it should be used together with its validation, unresolved-field and consistency reports, and quantitative values should
title: 756 Norwegian Oil and Gas License relinquishment reports with associated prospect leads and ideas extracted as canonical JSON files for consistent database entry

summary: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
title: SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report

summary: Analysis code and pre-specified analysis plan for the study "Beyond Pooled Accuracy: Hospital-Level Validation of Smartphone Image-Based Anaemia Screening in Pregnant Women". The package contains Python scripts for data integrity checks, colour feature extraction, frozen image-encoder features (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DINOv2, BiomedCLIP), the pre-specified models, nested model selection over 73 configurations, the site-identification test, a protocol-matched comparison with a published study, and a simulation study of site-related inflation of pooled AUC. The analysis plan (version 2, with dated amendments) is included. No participant data or images are included. Participants did not consent to public sharing of their data, including de-identified data. The simulation script runs without participant data.                                     This record contains the analysis plan and code for the study "Does smartphone AI see anaemia or the hospital? Validation in pregnant women in Uzbekistan" (Islomova, Nishanova and Qodirov; manuscript under review). The study tested whether smartphone photographs of the eyelid, tongue, lips, nail bed and palm can screen pregnant women for anaemia, and whether reported accuracy reflects anaemia or the hospital where the photographs were taken. It compared accuracy pooled across two hospitals in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, with accuracy inside each hospital, used a simulation in which images carry no anaemia information, and repeated the main checks in a public conjunctival dataset. Version 1 contains: - the pre-specified analysis plan, written before modelling, with dated amendments; - all analysis code for the two-hospital study, including the simulation code, which runs without participant data. Version 2 adds the replication in the public Eyes-defy-anemia dataset: - Eyes_Defy_tahlil_rejasi.md: the replication analysis plan, written before any result was computed; - Eyes_Defy_tahlil_kodi.py: the replication code; - Eyes_Defy_natijalar.txt: the full output of the replication analysis; - a table of derived colour features (55 values per record: RGB, CIELAB and HSV statistics, chromaticity and channel ratios), computed from the conjunctival masks after erosion by 3 pixels; - README.md: file descriptions, run order and software requirements. Participant data are not included. Women in the two-hospital study did not consent to public sharing of their data, including de-identified data. Requests for access for verification may be sent to the corresponding author (m.islomova@tuit.uz) and require approval by the ethics committee. Source dataset: Eyes-defy-anemia, IEEE DataPort, https://doi.org/10.21227/t5s2-4j73, released under CC BY 4.0. The derived colour
title: Analysis code and plan: Hospital-level validation of smartphone image-based anaemia screening in pregnant women

summary: Reproducible v3 benchmark archive accompanying the research manuscript “CRISPR-TRIAGE: Multi-Seed Benchmarking and Parameter-Efficient Bi-Modal Neural Prioritisation of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Target Cleavage Under Constrained Screening Budgets” (Rashid Kadayil, Pondicherry University). What is new in v3.0.0 (superseding v1.0.0): Expanded from single-seed two-cohort evaluation to a five-seed ( s ∈ {42, 123, 456, 789, 1011}), three-cohort, exact-sequence guide-disjoint benchmark across Listgarten 2018 GUIDE-seq, deduplicated K562, and deduplicated HEK293T ( N = 31 cleavage-positive guides, 249,768 candidate records, 237 detected positives within a 417,833-record, 41-guide universe; 16 model and ablation configurations). Principal pooled results: controlled reference CRISPR-TRIAGE (Full) (35,409 parameters) achieves 0.6899 Macro Recall@20 (Micro 0.5949), 0.8569 Recall@50, 0.9225 Recall@100, and 0.4484 Macro AP; 11-fold smaller Tabular-Only MLP (RankLoss) (3,217 parameters) achieves 0.6791 Recall@20 ( p = 0.7843); exploratory post-hoc pure-mismatch training ( No-Bulge Train , excluding 252,879 gap-containing CIRCLE-seq alignments) reaches 0.7243 Recall@20 ( p = 0.0022, p Holm = 0.0111). Archive contents ( crispr_triage_reproducible_release.zip , 38.71 MB, 233 files): Complete Python/PyTorch source code and post-hoc sensitivity audit scripts ( src/ , scripts/ ). 65 saved five-seed model checkpoints across 13 neural and gradient-boosted configurations plus 10 seed-fitted StandardScaler artifacts . Derived K562 and HEK293T cellular cohorts, Supplementary Tables S1–S7 (Online Resources 1–7), post-hoc audit CSVs, and complete upstream provenance/SHA-256 manifests ( DATA_MANIFEST.csv , RUN_MANIFEST.json verifying 232 registered artifacts, ENVIRONMENT_LOCK.txt ). Automated clean-room verification suite ( pytest tests/ -v : 12/12 tests passing offline with zero external downloads). Archive SHA-256: 7eaad446ca848d4475c037ecd530f7990daec5893553339a1b031b1314ce5850 . License: Original CRISPR-TRIAGE code and checkpoints under the MIT License; bundled third-party components and derived datasets retain their respective upstream licenses (see LICENSE and README.md ).
title: CRISPR-TRIAGE: Multi-Seed Benchmarking and Parameter-Efficient Bi-Modal Neural Prioritisation of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Target Cleavage Under Constrained Screening Budgets

summary: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation

summary: Lithography is a critical step in the manufacturing of chips that works by projecting light through a patterned mask and subsequently focusing it onto a photosensitive layer on top of a wafer. The task of finding a mask that prints a desired pattern on the wafer is called inverse lithography technology (ILT). The design of the mask is complicated by the fact that it must satisfy a set of constraints in order to be manufacturable. In this paper we provide a mathematical characterization of these constraints. Next, we develop a scoring function that allows us to measure whether a given mask satisfies the manufacturing constraints and if not, how badly the constraints are violated. Since our scoring function is (sub-)differentiable it can be used as the regularizer in a gradient-based inverse problem solver. We show that the resulting MorphILT algorithm that we developed can generate manufacturable masks that have nearly the same print quality as the (unmanufacturable) masks obtained from unconstrained inverse lithography.
title: A Morphological Approach to Inverse Lithography

summary: Overview This reproducibility package (Version 2.2) accompanies the manuscript entitled “Evaluating Conclusion Stability in SDG Classification: A Provenance-Aware Multi-Model Benchmark of Higher-Education Web Data.” The study extends the evaluation layer of a broader Enumeration-First Information Systems research framework developed for the acquisition and mapping of institutional digital artifacts to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Within this research context, Institutional Host Space (IHS) provides an operational abstraction of institutional web sources, while the present study focuses on the downstream evaluation of SDG classification outcomes. Research Objective The objective is to examine the sensitivity and stability of classifier conclusions under different benchmark constructions, reference-evidence policies, and inferential resampling units. The proposed Evaluation–Conclusion Stability Framework (ECSF) serves as an operational reporting and diagnostic framework that distinguishes five non-interchangeable components of scientific conclusions: model ranking, paired effect magnitude, interval-based inferential decisions, uncertainty precision, and reference-evidence sufficiency. Empirical Scope The study draws on a frozen archive of 20,098 digital artifacts collected from 51 Indonesian higher-education institutions. Four recovered classifier configurations are evaluated: M0: Rule-based SDG classification. M1: TF-IDF with Linear Support Vector Classification. M2: Multilingual sentence embeddings. M3: Multilingual DistilBERT. The evaluation uses two operational benchmarks (A0: 328 artifacts; A1: 400 artifacts), two reference-evidence policies (B0 and B1), and two resampling units (artifact-level and institution-cluster bootstrap). B0 retains insufficient evidence (NSE) as an explicit human-reference outcome and evaluates fixed-18 Macro-F1, whereas B1 excludes human-NSE records and evaluates fixed-17 Macro-F1. These policies define distinct evaluation estimands. Main Findings The descriptive model ranking remained unchanged across the four benchmark-policy states. However, four of twelve cross-benchmark pairwise contrast-shift confidence intervals excluded zero under the recorded exploratory procedure. Across 24 fixed-prediction comparisons, eleven institution-cluster bootstrap intervals were wider and thirteen were narrower than their artifact-level counterparts. Twenty-three comparisons produced concordant zero-exclusion decisions, while one comparison produced a discordant decision at an unchanged point estimate. The H400 reference ledger recorded agreement between two label columns for 393 of 400 artifacts, with adjudication documented for the remaining seven cases (Cohen's kappa = 0.977). These findings demonstrate that observed ranking stability does not necessarily imply stability across all components of classifier evaluation conclusions. Package Contents The package supports the reproducibility and auditability of the reported derived analyses through: Derived evaluation datasets and result tables. Frozen reference and prediction outputs. Analysis scripts and archived bootstrap result ledgers. De-identified reference-label traceability records. Benchmark and evidence-policy documentation. Scoped duplicate-sensitivity and lexical-retrieval audit results. Execution protocols and SHA-256 checksum manifests. README, data dictionary, citation metadata, and version history. Package integrity and reproducibility verification documentation. Version 2.2 aligns the package documentation and citation metadata with the accompanying manuscript while preserving the frozen empirical data, model outputs, analysis scripts, and reported experimental results. Reproducibility and Limitations The package supports derived evaluation and audit reproducibility, including the recalculation of selected evaluation metrics, verification of archived result ledgers, reference-label reconciliation, and integrity chec
title: Reproducibility Package for Evaluating Conclusion Stability in SDG Classification: A Provenance-Aware Multi-Model Benchmark of Higher-Education Web Data

summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.
title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering

summary: See the README.md of the individual crates for their own changelogs. The crates are now grouped into core , language , rewriter and transition_systems directories. This release adds a native type checker for the mCRL2 specification language. The new merc_typecheck crate type checks data specifications, including overload resolution, implicit numeric coercions, structured sorts and the polymorphic system-defined containers. The syntax tree now carries span information, which gives precise error messages and is the basis for a language server. Parsing of deeply nested if-then-else expressions is no longer quadratic. The new merc_explore crate provides a generic explicit state space exploration framework, with optional caching of summand enumeration, a control flow graph analysis and parallel (work stealing) exploration. It is used by merc-lps explore-explicit , by the PBES exploration and by merc-lts combine . The latter now caches enabled actions and shares action labels, which makes it considerably faster. The merc_ldd crate has been removed in favour of the LDD implementation of OxiDD . Symbolic reachability in merc-symbolic now supports chaining and saturation (following Ciardo) and summand grouping. The merc-pbes tool has been extended considerably. It can now explore PBES explicitly or symbolically into parity games, and solve them ( solve , solve-symbolic ). The merc-rewrite tool can now parse full mCRL2 specifications and has a new check command to type check data specifications. merc-lts supports the binary LTS formats where sensible, no longer converts i to tau when reading AUT files, and requires an output for convert . The explicit parity games and LTSs use compressed vectors to reduce memory usage. The merc_aterm crate has been reviewed to ensure that safe code cannot lead to undefined behaviour. In particular, Protected containers are now written through a scoped closure. Terms and function symbols have a more compact layout, the term parser no longer depends on pest, and garbage collection marking uses pointer tagging instead of a hash set. summary: This academic curriculum module delivers an analytical, physical, and computational exposition of satellite technology, Keplerian orbital mechanics, communications link budgets, and spacecraft subsystems across Low Earth Orbit (LEO), Medium Earth Orbit (MEO), and Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) environments. Key Technical Topics & Curricular Areas Covered: 1. Orbital Mechanics & Mission Design: Circular velocity derivations (v = sqrt(mu/r)), Kepler's Third Law orbital period determinations, Geostationary altitude sizing, and two-impulse Hohmann transfer delta-v maneuvers. 2. Space Communications & RF Link Budgets: Free-space path loss (FSPL) formulations across C-band, Ku-band, and Ka-band frequencies; antenna gain trade-offs; receiver noise figure thresholds; and rain fade atmospheric attenuation. 3. Satellite Subsystems Architecture: Attitude Determination and Control Systems (ADCS) using reaction wheels and magnetorquers; space power systems utilizing photovoltaic arrays and battery storage under orbital eclipse cycling; and thermal management via radiators and multi-layer insulation (MLI). 4. Modern Computational & AI-Era Paradigms: Machine-learning-augmented orbital perturbation propagators (ML-SGP4) correcting for solar-storm atmospheric drag surges; deep reinforcement learning for autonomous in-orbit collision avoidance; and edge AI hyperspectral compression on space-grade FPGAs. 5. Contemporary Systems Engineering Trade-offs: LEO mega-constellations vs. GEO wide-area platforms, optical inter-satellite links (ISLs) vs. RF ground relays, electric Hall-effect thrusters vs. chemical monopropellants, and standardized CubeSat modularity vs. high-reliability radiation-hardened redundancy. 6. Relativistic Physics in Space Systems: Gravitational time dilation and special relativity corrections essential for sub-meter Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). 7. Pedagogical Features: An interactive web-based orbit velocity and orbital period calculator with dynamic trajectory visualization, structured conceptual reviews, and step-by-step worked numerical engineering problems with explicit physical units. Format: Open Educational Resource (OER) prepared for persistent archiving on Zenodo and indexing in MERLOT. Permanent Webpage URL: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/aerospace-and-aeronautical-engineering/satellite-technology/
title: Satellite Technology Explained: Systems, Communication & Space Applications

summary: We present the AI Safety Formalization Atlas (AISFA), an open Lean 4 library and ledger that together form a shared epistemic infrastructure for AI safety mathematics: a record of what is proved, from which hypotheses and against which source, with rules for what may enter it. The Atlas has three aims. It formalizes AI safety results that often start as informal arguments. Where it can, it strengthens them, usually by proving them over wider classes of objects or under weaker hypotheses, and occasionally with sharper conclusions. It makes these very different results interoperable, so that they can be composed and a result proved in one domain can be transferred to another. We describe it to invite collaborators. The library holds about 200,000 lines of kernel-checked Lean. AI coding agents wrote the Atlas’s own Lean, and people check the critical points. Each statement that transcribes a published claim is graded against its printed wording: of 316 graded, 201 are stated more generally than print, and eighteen printed claims in twelve sources proved false as printed, each refuted in Lean beside a proved repair. One knowability interface carries impossibility results of one shape across six domains. As a public verifier for nine community solutions to Math for AI Safety open problems, the Atlas checked four, found three partial and two conditional.  Repository: https://github.com/mbrcic/ai-safety-formalization-atlas. Site: https://mbrcic.github.io/ai-safety-formalization-atlas/
title: The AI Safety Formalization Atlas: a machine-checked memory for AI safety mathematics

summary: This work introduces Theorem 81 — Constitutive Closure of Cosmological Expansion , developed within the Trinamica CP364 framework, with the aim of establishing a mathematical connection between elastic time dynamics and cosmological evolution. The research forms part of the CP364 scientific programme and constitutes a mathematical extension of the dossier HUBBLE CP364 — Foundations of Trinamica and Active Time Dynamics (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20666751). Theorem 81 introduces a constitutive structure in which elastic temporal deformation, active energy, temporal tension, coherence, and process memory contribute to defining the dynamic state of the system and its cosmological evolution. The formalization integrates three fundamental levels: Constitutive level: elastic temporal deformation, active energy, tension, and coherence. Dynamic level: Transition Regime (RT), elastic temporal memory, coupling, and process dynamics. Cosmological level: constitutive scale function, Hubble parameter, and connection with cosmological observables. The work distinguishes two levels of mathematical formalization: Theorem 81A — Conditional Kinematic Closure Establishes the conditions under which a positive and differentiable constitutive function of the trinamical state can represent the cosmological scale factor and yield the expansion parameter through its logarithmic derivative with respect to cosmic time. Problem 81B — Dynamic Constitutive Closure Defines the mathematical programme required to determine the cosmological constitutive function through CP364 evolution laws, RT–TEC compatibility, dynamic coupling, initial conditions, and process memory. The formalization includes: The distinction between elastic time, the evolutionary parameter of the Transition Regime, and cosmic time. The mathematical connection between the Transition Regime (RT) and the Trinamical Field Equations (TEC). The relationship between active energy, deformation, and elastic temporal tension. The introduction of an elastic response with a saturation function. The differential formalization of temporal coherence. The integration of elastic temporal memory into constitutive dynamics. The distinction between tensional decay, observational variation, and dynamic coupling. The definition of a candidate family of CP364 cosmological models. The formulation of the expansion parameter H_CP364(t) and its connection with H_CP364(z). The connection with redshift, luminosity distance, and distance modulus. The conditions for existence, regularity, saturation, and transitions between different evolutionary branches. The central contribution of Theorem 81 lies in the construction of a mathematical bridge between the internal dynamics of the Φ domain and the cosmological representation of expansion, while maintaining an explicit distinction between local constitutive quantities, process dynamics, and cosmological observables. From this perspective, cosmological expansion is investigated as a possible manifestation of a structural process in which temporal deformation, energy, coherence, and memory contribute to the evolution of the system. The resulting mathematical structure provides a foundation for the development of quantitative CP364 cosmological models that can be numerically integrated, parameterized, and compared with observational data. The research programme includes the determination of the remaining constitutive laws, parameter identification, analysis of critical regimes and bifurcations, comparison with reference cosmological models using the same datasets, and prospective validation through independent samples. The methodology maintains a clear separation between the different levels of investigation: Observed Data → Mathematical Transformations → Quantitative Results → CP364 Interpretation → Predictive Validation. Theorem 81 represents a further component of the mathematical edifice of Trinamica CP364 and establishes
title: HUBBLE CP364 - Teorema 81 - Chiusura Costitutiva dell'Espansione Cosmologica: Formalizzazione Matematica di H_CP364(z)

summary: Being • Becoming • Beyond the Classroom The title of the conference proposes a sequence and a challenge. Being asks who our students are before formal education begins: their languages, memories, families, social relationships, intellectual curiosity and sense of dignity. Becoming asks what education makes possible: learning, confidence, judgment, competence, agency and the courage to imagine alternative futures. Beyond the Classroom asks where those capacities will be exercised. The answer must include the home, the village, the market, the workplace, public institutions and the natural environment. The Santal Parganas region is an especially meaningful setting for this conversation. The six districts of Dumka, Deoghar, Godda, Jamtara, Pakur and Sahibganj are home to many communities and languages, including strong Santal traditions of land, social life, artistic expression and collective memory. Young people in the region encounter the opportunities of higher education alongside economic and geographical obstacles: variable transport access, family responsibilities, limited availability of some courses, digital connectivity and language differences. A regional conference therefore cannot define educational progress only in terms of examination results or numbers enrolled. It must ask whether students can remain in education, learn well, exercise genuine choice and carry their skills into forms of work and citizenship that they themselves value. A degree is significant, but its meaning is diminished if acquiring it requires a student to abandon all confidence in the community from which they come. The conference’s central proposition Education becomes socially transformative when it enlarges human capability while respecting cultural inheritance, promoting critical inquiry and strengthening responsibility for other persons and the environment. The papers in this book test that proposition in different ways, from Indigenous knowledge and climate justice to AI, conflict prevention, women’s participation, entrepreneurship, educational continuity and language learning
title: Being, Becoming and Beyond Classroom: International Conference Book of Abstracts

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Several forecasters each give a probability for the same yes/no event (rain tomorrow, a patient relapsing, an election). Each has seen different evidence and reports honestly. The best combination is the probability of the event given all the reports together, but that depends on how the forecasters' evidence overlaps, which is unknown. An aggregator has to learn it from a track record of past cases with known outcomes. This paper asks how long that track record must be. What was known. Lin and Chen (NeurIPS 2023) set up the model: n experts, each with at most m possible signals, exact calibrated reports, and T past cases. For experts whose evidence is independent given the outcome they showed that between about log(1/δ)/ε and 1/ε 2 cases are needed for accuracy ε; for arbitrary dependence, between about m n−2 /ε and m n /ε 2 . They conjectured that 1/ε is the right dependence and asked about the middle ground. Under conditional independence the ideal combination is the classical multiplicative pooling formula (their Lemma 5.1, credited to Bordley). Main result. Let η bound the conditional total correlation of the reports given the outcome: how much the experts share beyond what each knows about the outcome. With failure probability δ ≤ 1/32, the minimax excess Brier risk is of order min{1, log(1/δ)/T + min(η, m n /T)}, up to universal constants. So about log(1/δ)/ε cases are needed and suffice for conditionally independent experts, and about (m n + log(1/δ))/ε under arbitrary dependence, which raises the earlier m n−2 lower bound to m n . One estimator attains the rate without knowing η: fit the pooling formula, fit a lookup table, and keep whichever does better on held-out cases. The hard examples keep every expert's calibration curve, the prior and the whole distribution of report vectors fixed, so the difficulty lies in interactions that no single expert's track record reveals. Further results: the rate when the prior is known, impossibility of uniform consistency with unbounded report alphabets under any fixed dependence allowance, and an extension to finitely many outcomes. Relation to standard tools. For conditionally independent experts, localised-complexity arguments already give the upper bound up to a factor log T; the new parts there are removing that factor and the matching lower bounds. The main new content is the dependence trade-off and the calibrated worst-case construction. Limits. Reports are exact, honest, calibrated posteriors; rounding to whole percentages is not covered. The bounds are worst case over all laws (a particular group of forecasters may be much easier) and the constants are not optimised. With k outcomes, a factor of about k between the upper and lower bounds remains open. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); an exact-arithmetic verification script for the finite algebra of the constructions (9075 checks, standard library) and a small illustrative simulation, with their recorded outputs; the bibliography, a machine-readable index, a research-gate record, a review summary, a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Every check exits with an error on failure, also under python -O. Assurance. Written proofs; the scripts check finite algebra only. Internal AI-assisted review only: a combined five-role Claude review, the lead's exact checks with a negative control and a small simulation, one revision round, then a re-review and a proof audit of the new and rewritten proofs. No Astra/Codex review took place. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Learning to aggregate Bayesian forecasts: optimal sample complexity under bounded dependence

summary: Overview ChaosFlow is a configuration-driven research platform for evaluating fault recovery, operational resilience, and data integrity in distributed Big Data pipelines integrating Apache Kafka, Apache Spark Structured Streaming, Apache Hadoop HDFS, and Docker. This research dataset documents controlled fault-injection experiments investigating the distinction between infrastructure recovery, service readiness, application progress, sustained-throughput recovery, and independently verified output correctness. Experimental Design The experimental protocol covers eight scenarios: C0: No Fault C1: Kafka Container Stop C2: Kafka Container Restart C3: Spark Worker Failure C4: HDFS DataNode Failure C5: Network Fault C6: Storage Pressure C7: Checkpoint-Related Fault Each scenario is evaluated under observer-enabled and observer-disabled configurations, with 15 qualifying repetitions per experimental cell. The primary campaign records 240 qualifying observations and 16 additional invalid attempts. The broader research includes an independently executed second-machine evaluation, documented in the corresponding experimental evidence. Dataset and Correctness Verification The experimental workload consists of 1,000,000 input records, yielding 966,002 expected output occurrences after deterministic cleaning and filtering. Data correctness is assessed through independent schema-aware typed-row multiset verification and production validation. The research distinguishes successful qualifying executions from invalid attempts, including fault-exposed executions with incomplete output. Research Objectives The evidence supports investigation of: Differences between infrastructure, service, application, and throughput recovery. Data correctness following infrastructure fault injection. Monitoring and observer overhead. Recovery measurement sensitivity and censored observations. Experimental reproducibility across physical computing environments. Limitations of container-health indicators as evidence of application and data recovery. Research Artifacts The deposited materials provide the available experimental records, correctness-validation evidence, recovery measurements, statistical analyses, and supporting audit documentation included in this release. The dataset is intended to support independent research verification, reproducibility, and further investigation of distributed data-pipeline resilience. Limitations The reported findings are conditional on the specified experimental topology, workload, qualification criteria, and recovery-measurement definitions. Qualifying-run correctness does not imply unconditional correctness across all execution attempts.
title: ChaosFlow: Experimental Evidence and Replication Dataset for Distributed Pipeline Fault Recovery

summary: This repository holds the reference Python implementation of TRUST-Balance (Trustworthy Risk-adaptive Utility and STructure-preserving Balancing), a model-agnostic framework for imbalanced classification. TRUST-Balance treats class-imbalance handling as risk-constrained intervention selection rather than fixed resampling. It splits the minority class into regions with K-means. For each region it chooses between screened synthetic generation, localised reweighting and abstention, scoring each candidate by its estimated reduction in class-balanced validation risk. That score is penalised for uncertainty, structural distortion and cost, and is subject to a tolerance on majority-class loss. The procedure stops when no intervention gives a positive utility. The estimator is scikit-learn compatible and works with any probabilistic classifier. It has three optional modes: a post-selection refit (TRUST+R), a Hoeffding-type acceptance certificate (TRUST-C), and subsampled screening that scales to millions of records. The archive contains the estimator and re-implementations of three recent adaptive baselines (ART, UGO and GDEO). It also includes a script that downloads the 27 public benchmark datasets from KEEL, PMLB/UCI and scikit-learn, plus the full experimental pipeline. The pipeline benchmarks logistic regression, random forests and XGBoost against 13 competing approaches, including the unmodified model. It also runs ablation, safeguard stress tests, sensitivity, robustness to imbalance ratio, label noise and class overlap, multiclass extension, certification and scalability studies up to one million records. The archive also ships the raw per-run results as CSV, the summary tables, the figures, and analysis scripts that reproduce every table and figure of the accompanying article. Those statistics include Friedman/Iman–Davenport tests, Nemenyi critical differences and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests. Code is released under the MIT licence and results under CC BY 4.0. Keywords: imbalanced classification; class imbalance; adaptive resampling; oversampling; SMOTE; cost-sensitive learning; risk-constrained optimisation; utility-guided learning; minority-class recognition; probability calibration; statistical certification; scalability; big data analytics; machine learning; Python; scikit-learn
title: TRUST-Balance: a risk-constrained, utility-guided learning framework for adaptive and scalable imbalanced classification

summary: We establish and assemble explicit algebraic, arithmetic and analytic properties of parameterized compositional inverses. We also resolve the recorded binomial-sum conjecture for A063019 and establish the exact forms of its other recorded mathematical statements. The results include a two-step effective recurrence for a cubic inverse family, Jacobi and Gegenbauer parameter-root descriptions, exact modular-Dyck first negative reversals, prime-index congruences, finite-field parity laws, Frobenius divisibility for Hankel matrices, infinite sign changes, an exact asymptotic sign-density law, strict parameter-index total positivity of order two, and boundaries for moment positivity. The proofs are carried out at the stated parameter and index ranges, using formal Lagrange inversion, finite-field algebra, orthogonal polynomials, and singularity analysis. A correspondence table for 46 named sequences and exact worked examples make the parameter specializations and the available finite verification independently reproducible. Classical inversion techniques, published single-sequence formulas, and earlier orthogonal-polynomial and moment results retain their prior attribution. Licensing note: The manuscript is licensed under CC BY 4.0. The OEIS b-file snapshots included in the supplementary archive retain their original CC BY-SA 4.0 license and attribution. The independently authored verification code is made available under CC BY 4.0.
title: Structural Theorems for Parameter Families of Algebraic Series Reversions

summary: Epigrass 5.0.1 Patch release: epirunner no longer destroys the contents of your Redis server. 🐛 Bug fixes Stopped wiping the default Redis at startup — epirunner used to call FLUSHALL on the hardcoded localhost:6379 on every run, destroying any unrelated data living there ( a751775 ). Startup cleanup now deletes only Epigrass' own keys (see below). --view-only fixed — closing a view-only dashboard no longer falls through into a full simulation run, and view-only mode no longer requires a Redis server at all. Clear failure when Redis is unreachable — Simulate() now fails early with configuration hints instead of a bare assert at import time. ✨ Improvements Redis connection is configurable via environment variables — replaces the hardcoded localhost:6379 used by three independent clients: EPIGRASS_REDIS_URL — full connection URL ( redis://... , rediss://... , unix://... ) or individually: EPIGRASS_REDIS_HOST , EPIGRASS_REDIS_PORT , EPIGRASS_REDIS_DB All state keys are namespaced under epigrass: (configurable via EPIGRASS_REDIS_PREFIX ), so Epigrass is safe to share a Redis server with other applications. The TUI's Redis status check honors the same environment configuration. Redis configuration documented in the installation docs. ⬆️ Upgrade notes If you run Epigrass against a shared Redis server, no action is needed — Epigrass will only ever read and delete its own epigrass:* keys. To point it at a dedicated server: export EPIGRASS_REDIS_URL="redis://myserver:6379/0"

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: VasQ v1.0.0 is the software release of VasQ, accompanying the manuscript Atlas of regional molecular specialization in the human brain vasculature. VasQ is an AI chat system for exploring a single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of the human brain vasculature (41 brain regions, about 443,000 nuclei from four donors). It helps users generate hypotheses about blood–brain barrier biology, regional vascular specialization and drug delivery. This release contains: Web application (Django): classifies each question and routes it to the right workflow. Expression statistics are calculated directly from the log-normalized atlas matrix: mean expression, percentage of expressing cells and cell counts. Groups with fewer than 10 cells are excluded. Results come with interactive plots, tables and CSV downloads. A batch mode takes up to 20 questions and saves a PDF report for each. Only aggregate results are passed to the language model, never the matrix or individual-cell records. Evidence retrieval: gene, disease, pathway and drug evidence with source links, including a knowledge-graph retrieval module built on the SPOKE knowledge graph. Evaluation scripts: for query-intent classification and entity extraction, as reported in the manuscript. Docker configurations: for local use and for deployment on Railway. The hosted version is free to use with no login: https://vasq-production-65c6.up.railway.app/vasq/. To run VasQ locally you need Docker, your own OpenAI API key and three expression data files from Figshare (https://figshare.com/projects/Atlas_of_Regional_Molecular_Specialization_in_the_Human_Brain_Vasculature/273930). Setup instructions and example queries are in the README. VasQ is intended for research exploration and hypothesis generation, not clinical decision-making. The software is released under the Apache License 2.0. Its design was informed by scChat and KG-RAG.

summary: REPLICATION PACKAGE Financial language, self-assessed and objective financial knowledge Data and code for: "Perceived difficulty of financial language and the confidence-competence gap". Manuscript submitted to Finance Research Letters. CONTENTS data/fin_language_knowledge_extract.sav     Anonymized extract (SPSS format, with value labels). data/fin_language_knowledge_extract.csv     The same data as CSV (UTF-8, comma-separated, empty cell = missing). code/spss/*.sps     All analyses as SPSS syntax (run 00_przygotowanie.sps first).     Script used to create the extract from the full survey file (for     transparency; the full file is not shared). DATA Three-wave online panel of Polish adults (ReaktorOpinii.pl research panel, random-quota sample by sex, age and place of residence), fielded by Instytut Badań Pollster: Wave 1 N = 4,389; Wave 2 N = 2,729; Wave 3 N = 1,955. One row per respondent; variables from Waves 2 and 3 are missing for respondents who did not take part in those waves. The extract contains only the variables used in the article (83 of about 1,450 in the full questionnaire): - perceived financial-language difficulty (Wave 1); - self-assessed financial knowledge (three waves; each respondent saw one   of three randomly assigned grammatical wordings); - 18-item financial-knowledge test, item level (three waves); - 8-item numeracy test, item level (Wave 1); - education, household income, sex, age; - randomized design variables (questionnaire version, Wave 1 group,   financial-education material between Waves 1 and 2); - post-stratification weight for Wave 3. Anonymization. The panel identifier was replaced by a random pseudonymous ID that cannot be linked to the panel. Age is top-coded at 80. Open-ended answers, place of residence, region and all variables not used in the article were removed. Top-coding age changes no reported estimate at the third decimal place. Access is granted to researchers for non-commercial academic research. Requests should state the intended use. Users agree not to attempt to re-identify respondents, not to redistribute the data, and to cite the dataset and the article.

summary: The repository contains post-processed data generated using the Large Fire Simulator, FSim, for three of the scenarios analyzed in the paper titled "High burn probability drives prescribed fire PM2.5 net benefits": the baseline scenario, and scenarios 1 and 2 (treating 28% and 20% of the landscape, respectively).  Probability rasters: the burn probability and conditional flame length probability rasters (six flame length categories), merged across fire occurrence areas (FOAs) covering Central Washington. Fire effects rasters:  expected fire effects (calculated with Equation 3, substituting any given effect for the emissions term) for a 15 km buffer around Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (OkaWen). Effects include volume mortality (cuft/acre killed in fire), percent basal area mortality (% of total basal area killed in fire), fuel consumption (tons/acre), PM2.5 emissions (tons/acre), total board feet lost (board feet - 144 in^3, and merchantable cubic feet lost (ft^3).  FOA-level post-processed outputs: for each scenario and FOA (1-3), the zip file contains 1) the list of fires simulated by FSim, including the area burned and the day and weather type, 2) a geodatabase of ignition points, 3) a geodatabase of fire perimeters, 4) a summary of seasonal fuel consumption and PM2.5 emissions for the 15-km buffered area around OkaWen, 5) a summary of seasonal fuel consumption and PM2.5 emissions for the full FOA, and 6) 20,000 mosaicked seasonal rasters of fire IDs, arrival days, fuel consumed, and PM2.5 emissions for all fires in each season (with overburn removed).
title: Sindewald et al - High burn probability drives prescribed fire PM2.5 net benefits - Part 1

Effects include volume mortality (cuft/acre killed in fire), percent basal area mortality (% of total basal area killed in fire), fuel consumption (tons/acre), PM2.5 emissions (tons/acre), total board feet lost (board feet - 144 in^3, and merchantable cubic feet lost (ft^3).  FOA-level post-processed outputs: for each scenario and FOA (1-3), the zip file contains 1) the list of fires simulated by FSim, including the area burned and the day and weather type, 2) a geodatabase of ignition points, 3) a geodatabase of fire perimeters, 4) a summary of seasonal fuel consumption and PM2.5 emissions for the 15-km buffered area around OkaWen, 5) a summary of seasonal fuel consumption and PM2.5 emissions for the full FOA, and 6) 20,000 mosaicked seasonal rasters of fire IDs, arrival days, fuel consumed, and PM2.5 emissions for all fires in each season (with overburn removed).
title: Sindewald et al - High burn probability drives prescribed fire PM2.5 net benefits - Part 1

summary: This article systematically examines the fundamental molecular and biochemical mechanisms underlying atherosclerosis progression, focusing on cholesterol homeostasis disruption, endogenous cholesterol biosynthesis ( HMG-CoA reductase  pathway), free radical-mediated oxidation of low-density lipoproteins ( LDL ), and foam cell formation. The study details the chain reactions of polyunsaturated fatty acid ( PUFA ) peroxidation within the subendothelial space, the structural modification of apolipoprotein B-100  ( ApoB-100 ) by reactive aldehydes such as malondialdehyde ( MDA ) and hydroxynonenal  ( HNE ), and intracellular cholesteryl ester accumulation catalyzed by ACAT-1 . Furthermore, the atheroprotective role of reverse cholesterol transport ( RCT ) mediated by high-density lipoproteins ( HDL ) and lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase ( LCAT ) is substantiated through specific biochemical reaction pathways.
tags: atherosclerosis, dyslipidemia, oxidized LDL (oxLDL), lipid peroxidation, HMG-CoA reductase, foam cells, ACAT-1, LCAT, reactive oxygen species, endothelial dysfunction.
title: BIOCHEMICAL MECHANISMS OF LIPID METABOLISM DISORDERS AND THE OXIDATION OF LOW-DENSITY LIPOPROTEINS (LDL) IN THE PATHOGENESIS OF ATHEROSCLEROSIS
