summary: We study the kink and particle spectra for the massive $φ_{2,1}$-deformations of minimal models $\mathcal M_{k+1,k+2}$ via truncated conformal space approach (TCSA) on a defect circle. The massive $φ_{2,1}$-deformation preserves a set of non-invertible symmetries, furnishing a fusion category $\mathcal C_k\simeq {\rm SO}(3)_k$. These non-invertible symmetries are spontaneously broken, and thus label the vacua and organize the kinks and particles into their multiplets in terms of quiver diagrams. We employ a finite-volume truncated Hamiltonian approach on defect Hilbert spaces, $\mathcal H_{X_i}$ for $X_i\in\mathcal C_k$, to study these quivers in the IR theories. The symmetry defect can then close an individual kink on a circle. We first establish the relation between states of definite fractional momentum on the defect circle and physical kink and particle states labelled by their vacuum pairs. Using form factors of local fields, we independently measure the squared amplitudes between the states of the two bases in defect TCSA. Combining these measurements with defect TCSA spectra, we reconstruct the quiver diagrams for $k=3,4,5$ without assuming them in advance. In particular, for $k=4$ we reconstruct the distinct quivers of the ordered and disordered phases. For $k=5$, we identify the quivers of both the light and heavy multiplets.
title: Reconstructing massive quivers on a defect circle

summary: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.
title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images

summary: We establish a reconstruction principle for Poisson random measures arising in compactness arguments for jump-driven stochastic partial differential equations. A basic difficulty in such arguments is that, after a Skorokhod-type representation, almost sure convergence of the solution processes does not by itself identify the limiting stochastic integral, since integration with respect to a compensated Poisson random measure is not a pathwise continuous functional of the solution and the noise. We address this problem in the variational framework of a Gelfand triple $V\hookrightarrow H\equiv H^\ast\hookrightarrow V^\ast$ for equations with locally monotone drift. Starting from a tight sequence of approximating solutions in $D([0,T];H)\cap L^α(0,T;V),$ we construct, on the represented probability space, a time-homogeneous Poisson random measure with the original Lévy intensity and compensator, compatible with the limiting filtration, such that the limiting process solves the corresponding SPDE. The main ingredient is a noise bridge. Together with a shifted dyadic approximation of the solution, the increments of the solution path over dyadic time cells approximate the compensated noise increments; since the time integral of the drift is continuous in $H$, no regularisation of the drift is needed. The jumps are then recovered by a measurable registration procedure, while injectivity of the jump coefficient permits reconstruction of the corresponding marks through a Borel inverse obtained from the Lusin--Suslin theorem. The reconstruction is performed simultaneously at all truncation levels; consistency of the resulting finite jump measures and a monotone patching argument yield a Poisson random measure with the full Lévy measure. Under the injectivity assumption, no enlargement of the represented probability space is required.
title: Reconstruction of Poisson Random Measures in the Variational Framework with Applications to Jump-Driven SPDEs

summary: Delocalized bonding electrons have long been associated with soft bonds and low phonon frequencies. However, a quantitative connection between electron delocalization and phonon softening remains elusive. We identify such a connection through the momentum-space quantum metric, which measures the intrinsic delocalization of the occupied electronic states. We show that a quantum geometric contribution to phonon softening is proportional to the integrated quantum metric. First-principles calculations of more than a hundred compounds demonstrate that greater quantum metric generally accompanies softer phonons. Localized Wannier orbitals reveal the bonding environments associated with this delocalization. In ferroelectric GeTe, LiBeSb, and BaTiO$_3$, polar distortion localizes the bonding orbitals, reduces quantum metric, and stabilizes the soft mode of the nonpolar structure. In PbSe, pressure-induced band inversion is accompanied by an enhanced quantum metric and phonon softening without change in crystal symmetry and bonding. These results establish a common quantum geometric interpretation of bond delocalization and phonon softening across distinct bonding environments.
title: Quantum Metric Connects Bond Delocalization to Phonon Softening

summary: Magnetic reconnection taps black-hole rotational energy via negative-energy ejecta, but field geometry itself can forbid such ejection inside the spacetime ergoregion. We identify a covariant electromagnetic (EM) ergoregion for general degenerate, magnetically dominated fields in stationary spacetimes. Outside the EM ergoregion, even ultrarelativistic field-guided ejecta cannot attain negative Killing energy. For Alfvénic reconnection outflows, the magnetization threshold scales inversely with the transverse distance to the EM ergosurface. The mass-loaded Kerr model places the EM ergosurface at about 75% of the radial interval from the horizon to the spacetime ergosurface, close to the time-averaged boundary inferred from a dynamical simulation. Together, these results show that field geometry determines where negative-energy ejection is possible, while magnetization sets the threshold for realizing it.
title: An Electromagnetic Ergoregion Limits the Reconnection-Driven Penrose Process

summary: We identify the galaxy cluster RM J121917.6+505432.8 as a candidate bimodal merging cluster due to its optical properties listed in the redMaPPer cluster catalog. To confirm the cluster's merging state and reveal its dark matter halo and intracluster medium (ICM) morphologies, we conducted a multiwavelength follow-up campaign encompassing HST/ACS optical observations, XMM-Newton X-ray imaging, and Keck/Deimos multislit spectroscopy. The weak lensing mass reconstruction performed with the HST images shows two resolved peaks whose positions coincide with the two brightest cluster galaxies. The ICM morphology is consistent with a post-pericenter merger, with significant asymmetry in X-ray flux between subclusters. Our Keck/Deimos redshift measurements reveal a relative velocity $Δv_{\mathrm{LOS}} = 480$ km s$^{-1}$ between eastern and western subclusters. The eastern, more massive subcluster, however, exhibits a highly elongated shape, suggesting either a dark matter halo of considerable eccentricity or the presence of a third, unresolved halo, eliciting the question of whether RMJ1219 is truly binary or a three-way merger. To investigate these hypotheses, we fit the weak lensing shear data using four different combinations of spherical and elliptical NFW halo models and provide an estimate of the mass and concentration of each subhalo. Although the best fit is achieved with a three-halo model, the data are insufficient to determine whether the introduction of extra parameters is statistically justified.
title: Multiwavelength Analysis of the Merging Cluster RM J121917.6+505432.8: A Three-way Merger in Disguise?

summary: A neutron detector placed outside a subcritical system records fission chains as correlated bursts of counts. The time dependence of these correlations gives access to the $α$ eigenvalues governing the decay of the system and, with additional physical information, to its effective multiplication factor $k_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The usual analysis relies on point kinetics, which ignores where chains are born and which neutrons escape. We examine this approximation in a model simple enough to be solved: branching Brownian motion, that is, one-group neutron diffusion with capture and fission, in a domain whose absorbing boundary plays the role of the detector. For a stationary Poisson source we derive the Feynman $Y$ function (the count variance-to-mean ratio minus one) by following pairs of neutrons from their common ancestor to their detection. In a homogeneous cube the result is an explicit sum over spatial modes whose weights are fixed by the geometry and the source. We compare it with direct branching simulations and with one-speed OpenMC transport calculations in which fission is sampled with analog reaction selection and FREYA multiplicities. At the longest simulated gate the model agrees with transport to about $1\%$ at $k=0.8$ and $0.9$, and to $10\%$ at $k=0.5$. The corresponding point-model discrepancies range from $25$ to $48\%$. When geometry, source and material parameters are known, retaining the spatial modes also reduces the bias on the inferred multiplication factor. Two extensions prepare the use of the model in inverse problems. Correlations between opposite faces distinguish systems that share the same fundamental decay rate but differ in leakage, and a hierarchy of three stationary problems links this spatial benchmark to multiplicity counting. Modal convergence, detector imbalance and spectral evolution remain limitations for quantitative inference.
title: Estimating subcritical multiplication from stochastic neutron noise: a branching Brownian motion model for leakage counts

summary: Replication code and derived numerical outputs for the manuscript Idle SOC placement in peak-shaving batteries: matched-throughput lifetime gains and retrofit-value boundaries by Limin Liu and Hong Wang. The archive includes dispatch reconstruction, nonlinear ageing replay, SOC-shape and cycling-exponent sensitivity, tariff-window analysis, chemistry-specific discounted cash-flow scenarios, cached inputs and figure-generation scripts. The LG M50 reference lifetime is independently replayed rather than inherited from LFP. Third-party cell-level raw datasets are not redistributed. The raw public-price CSV is excluded because the provider does not identify a redistribution licence; source metadata and checksum are supplied. This archive does not regenerate the historical Fig. 1 calibration from raw cell records and contains no dynamic-SOC experimental results.
title: Reproducibility archive for Idle SOC placement in peak-shaving batteries: matched-throughput lifetime gains and retrofit-value boundaries (v2.3)

summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The author's answer to Riemann's question is geometric: on each range chosen in a definite way, the process of the link of the primes is seen as the unit circle and a sinusoid around it; for his work the author regards this answer as a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and what in it is accepted as an initial prin

summary: This dataset provides reprocessed energetic proton and electron flux measurements from the Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES). The original satellite observations have been processed to derive differential particle fluxes, which are subsequently mapped to a reference altitude of 100 km. The dataset was developed to support the reconstruction and analysis of energetic particle flux distributions in the near-Earth space environment. The reprocessed observations serve as the primary data source for the development and evaluation of the machine learning model presented in the associated study.
title: Reprocessed POES Differential Proton and Electron Flux Dataset Mapped to 100 km Altitude

summary: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.
title: Not Every Input Needs Everything: Unifying Expert Gating, Model Cascades, and Agent Orchestration

summary: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.
title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation

summary: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.
title: Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments

summary: Although multi-agent deep reinforcement learning enables coordinated behavior, aligning it with managerial intent remains difficult due to complex agent interactions. Although the strategy-following distributed attentional actor architecture (sfDA7-X) improves controllability via regional instructions, instruction combinations scale exponentially with team and instruction sizes, leading to prohibitive training costs and poor transferability. To reduce this computational cost, we introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture and reconstruct collective behavior by replicating a single trained policy across agents in teams of different sizes, thereby eliminating the need to train from scratch. Additionally, we evaluate warm-start retraining by initializing policy networks with a pre-trained policy to significantly lower computational overhead. In an object collection game, a policy trained in a four-agent team is deployed to teams of three to eight agents. Experiments demonstrate that training with the proposed aggregated observation matrix achieves performance comparable to that of the baseline method, sfDA7-X. Furthermore, policy replication preserves performance without substantial degradation in three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining outperforms training from scratch while reducing required training episodes by up to 90%. Deployments to six- and eight-agent teams further confirm effective spatial region allocation following given instructions. These results demonstrate that the proposed method enables zero-shot collective behavior reconstruction via policy replication.
title: Post-Training Policy Replication for Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning across Team Sizes

summary: Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.
title: AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction

summary: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.
title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Under approval voting each voter ticks every acceptable candidate and the most ticks win. Under a positional scoring rule (Borda is the best-known) voters rank the candidates and positions earn points. A sincere voter switching from ticks to a ranking puts every approved candidate above every other one, but the order inside the two groups is free. Terzopoulou, Lang and Zwicker (Social Choice and Welfare, 2026) asked which scoring rules can always reproduce the approval winners for some such sincere rankings, when every ballot may be counted a fixed number of times. They showed Borda can, that no other rule can with three candidates, and asked whether Borda is unique for more candidates. Results. (1) Best–worst voting (one point for first place, minus one for last) makes exactly the approval winners win together, for every number m of candidates, with at most m − 1 copies of each ballot, and one voter can force that many. So Borda is not unique for any m ≥ 4, and the rule (2,1,1,0), which the original authors believed to work, does. (2) A polynomial-time test of the property for any rational scoring vector, a reflection-symmetry lemma, and complete lists of the rules with the property for four and five candidates and of the rational rules for six candidates (four: completes their necessary condition; five and six: new). (3) Their conjectured scalar criterion for electing one designated approval winner holds for every real scoring vector when a ballot may be split between rankings, and for every rational scoring vector under replication. (4) With whole copies and irrational scores it can fail: in an eight-candidate, five-ballot election the designated candidate can win exactly when a parameter of the rule is rational, and the copies needed can be arbitrarily many. Limits. The results concern the existence of sincere rankings, not what voters would submit, and hold for every electorate (worst case). Irrational six-candidate rules and a general formula for all numbers of candidates remain open. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF), three Python scripts (exact rational arithmetic: certificate checks for four, five and six candidates and the eight-candidate witness; the signed vertex cases with SymPy; exhaustive best–worst replication counts for three to five candidates), the certificate file, the bibliography, a machine-readable index, a research-gate record, a review summary, a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Assurance. Written proofs with exact computational checks. Internal AI-assisted review only: a combined Claude review panel, a revision round, a verification re-review, a proof audit and clean replays with a negative control. No Astra/Codex review took place. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Recovering approval winners from ranked ballots: best–worst voting and the approval-compatibility questions of Terzopoulou, Lang and Zwicker

summary: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.
title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures

summary: Code, data, raw simulation logs and analysis scripts for the paper "Certified Throughput Bounds for Warehouse Robot Fleets and a Long-Run Benchmark Audit". The artifact contains a lifelong multi-agent path finding simulator with a PIBT re-implementation and a conflict checker, elementary and linear-programming throughput bounds with independently checkable price certificates, the bridge count of every benchmark map, the raw logs of all simulation runs (including the 5,000-step runs that show gridlock on maps with bridges), representative cases and toy examples, and scripts that regenerate every table, figure and number of the paper and its supplementary material with one command (`bash reproduce.sh`; quick check in about one minute: `bash reproduce.sh quick`). Third-party maps and guidance graphs are redistributed under their own licenses (USC Research License for the two RHCR maps: non-commercial use only; MIT for the GGO maps and guidance graphs); see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md

summary: When LLM agents verify each other's work over a long interaction, they drift into collusion: they come to accept work without the evidence that the verification protocol requires. Collusion is absent at the start and builds up episode by episode, which we trace to accurate feedback accumulating in memory. An agent that follows the rule is told that its verdict was wrong whenever its peer was right, so breaking the rule is the reward-maximizing choice, and agents talk themselves into it in their private reflections. Existing mitigations leave the agents unchanged; we train the behavior out. PROVE (Protocol Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them rather than by their outcome, and credits every call an agent makes, including the calls that solve its own task, with the outcome that call controls. On Qwen3.6-27B, a LoRA adapter trained on six-episode interactions takes the collusion rate on held-out task sequences at the original ten-episode horizon from 65.0% to 1.0%, with no detectable change in task success. Collusion that converged in every interaction now converges in none, and the gain holds four episodes beyond the longest interaction seen in training. The trained 27B model colludes less than every model evaluated in the original study, closed-weight frontier models included. Code is available at https://github.com/Haochen-Luo/PROVE.
title: PROVE: Mitigating Long-Horizon LLM Collusion with Reinforcement Learning from Verified Evidence

summary: Retrieve-and-correct policies typically refine the nearest retrieved demonstration chunk, the readout that works best when executed directly. We study what a demonstration memory should supply to the corrector instead and find that a smooth, softmax-weighted recall over the whole memory is a much better base. On ALOHA cube transfer (40 human demonstrations), soft recall is no better to execute alone than the nearest chunk; however, with keys, candidates, and training fixed, correcting it raises success by 22.4 points on fresh resets with new encoders and by 7.4 against a closed-loop-tuned top-1 corrector. On robomimic Square, it leads by 7.9 points with the two better operators and by 6.7 on a label-free draw of equal size. This gain holds on sparse, varied demonstrations under an action-aware key and leave-one-demonstration-out training, and fades or slightly reverses on dense, scripted, or generated data. Building on this finding, our hetero-associative visuomotor memory (HAVM, 14M parameters) trains offline in about five minutes, including a learned retrieval temperature $β$, and runs in 1.1 ms. summary: Long sequence reconstruction must correct accumulated drift while preserving locally consistent geometry. In robotics and autonomous driving, embodied acquisition provides recurring platform- environment geometry and repeated observations of scene structure and platform motion. We present Embodied-VGGT, which exploits these cues to establish reliable local relationships and selectively preserve them during global refinement. Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) builds on Scal3R's global context memory and uses relative scale references derived from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, encouraging cross-chunk consistency while limiting changes to reliable local geometry. Superpoint Alignment (SA) and Cross-Loop Optimization (CL) jointly address the robust establishment and preservation of geometric relationships. SA balances ground and non-ground evidence across spatial regions to estimate inter-chunk translation. CL uses geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each receiving a shared Sim(3) correction that preserves its internal relative transformations during global optimization. Experiments on five public driving benchmarks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in long sequence reconstruction. On KITTI Odometry, Embodied-VGGT achieves a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% compared with the state-of-the-art baseline under same evaluation protocol. To facilitate reproducibility, we released our code: https://github.com/Ang-Sheep/Embodied-VGGT.
title: Embodied-VGGT: Preserving Reliable Local Geometry for Long-Sequence Reconstruction

summary: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.
title: Normalizing Flows are Capable World Models

summary: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.
title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions

summary: We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.
title: LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies

summary: Entanglement asymmetry has emerged as a powerful probe of symmetry restoration and the quantum Mpemba effect. However, its conventional Rényi generalizations, defined as differences of Rényi entropies, are not monotones in the resource-theoretic sense. Here, we investigate an alternative family of asymmetry quantifiers based on sandwiched Rényi divergences, which satisfy monotonicity under symmetry-preserving quantum channels. Developing a two-parameter replica approach, we show how these quantities can be computed from charged moments and establish a remarkable correspondence with conventional Rényi asymmetries under the inversion of the Rényi index, $α\leftrightarrow 1/α$. This relation, exact for pure states, holds at leading order in the relevant scaling limits for homogeneous quantum quenches, including interacting integrable systems, and for Haar-random states. Applying these results to quenches from tilted ferromagnetic states, we demonstrate that the quantum Mpemba effect is remarkably robust, occurring throughout the entire family of sandwiched Rényi asymmetry monotones. We identify dynamical regimes in quenches from spatially inhomogeneous initial states where conventional Rényi asymmetries and genuine monotones exhibit qualitatively different behaviours. We also investigate a solvable toy model illustrating the possible dependence of Mpemba crossings on the Rényi index. Our findings establish a connection between conventional Rényi asymmetries and quantum resource theory, explaining their effectiveness in broad classes of nonequilibrium protocols while highlighting the additional information provided by genuine asymmetry monotones.
title: Monotonic probes of asymmetry and robustness of the quantum Mpemba effect

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Fifty-one entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature, among them: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7; a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients; a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset; a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten; a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998); a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation; a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight; a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. Light through a Jerlov water type. The package: computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963); converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors; gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m, and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers; integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth; gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two; and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent; ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum; carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models; converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient. Measurements it carries. Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type, against which the depth profile is checked; Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille; the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures; Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters; five published spectra of the absorption of pure water, Pope & Fry (1997), Smith & Baker (1981), Mason, Cone & Fry (2016), Lee et al. (2015) and Morel et al. (2007), for the caller to choose from; the eight stations of the clearest ocean water measured, Morel et al. (2007); the measured reflectance of ten materials found in and around water, from the USGS Spectral Library Version 7, for reference images of how they look through each water type. Without a water type. It gives: Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001, and the earlier edition of Morel 1988), or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013); the attenuation of the visible and of the whole shortwave from the surface to a depth, and the depth where a given fraction of the visible light is left, the euphotic depth among them, from the absorption and backscattering coefficients at 490 nm and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2007); from chlorophyll, the absorption by phytoplankton (Bricaud et al. 1995) and t

summary: Data and code for a two-layer analysis of 75 documented Peranakan Nyonya porcelain objects. Layer 1 tests the decorative structure: co-occurrence of motifs against a fixed-margin Curveball null and the placement of each motif in the main field or border bands, coded independently by two coders. Layer 2 evaluates an aggregate cross-tradition score for motifs with documented tradition associations, split into a motif-level part and an object-level contrast. A representation audit applies a whole-part rule to decorative bands and sets and changes the network from 332 to 321 object-motif links; the archive contains every network version, the audit log, both coders' placement forms and all results, sensitivity analyses and figure code. It also keeps the evidence chain of earlier versions (object provenance, motif dictionary, coding manual, independent attribution coding, reliability, adjudication and evidence audit). Material used only by an earlier manuscript is retained unchanged under 99_SUPERSEDED. Museum images and source documents are not redistributed.

summary: Abstract What is new. The individual tools here are known: Fr´echet bands, Vorob’ev gluing, toric selection, Picard–Lefschetz moves. What is new is one geometric landscape in which a decision maker’s information state is a point that moves as evidence arrives, and every change it un- dergoes is located, typed and given a consequence. The credal fibre shows what the data leave open; the walls of the mirror potential show where the description changes; each wall is classified as forced or computed. A collision of critical values is forced: the two hypotheses are orthogonal and the crossing is canonical, in every fibre dimension. A caustic forces its intersection number, but the side from which it was approached is a convention the data cannot fix. A Stokes event carries intersection numbers that must be computed. Rings of contexts show where gluing fails and by how much. The history of the state records what can be committed at once and what must wait. The landscape is mapped completely for 2 × 3 tables, at the level of critical values for 3 × 4, and by calibration for 3 × 3. It explains how an information state flows; whether it also anticipates decisions earlier than simpler records is an open, registered question. The geometry in brief. A conditioned state is a geometric object. The laws compatible with what has been observed form a polytope, the credal fibre. Its faces are cut out by the cells of the tables, and its vertices are certified by bases that come in dual pairs: the positive cells of a vertex form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph of the table (a graphic-matroid basis), and the zero cells form the complementary cographic basis, whose normals span the vertex cone. Conditioning maps the fibre onto a polytope of conditional laws, and the probability bands we report are coordinate projections of that polytope. Evidence acts on it by a projective map, an isometry of the Hilbert metric. Sampling noise is described differently: under regular sampling conditions it is asymptotically a Fisher–Rao confidence region, whose square-root image on the round sphere is approximately a spherical cap of radius of order m−1/2. Toric K¨ahler geometry supplies the selected law inside the fibre, its scales and its walls; the chamber complex of the margins supplies the stratification along which all of this changes. The note develops this picture and tests every computable claim against exact, pre-registered checks. A running example. A water authority must decide whether to keep seeding storms with silver iodide. It continues if q = P (above-normal rain | seeded, wet forecast) is at least a cost ratio θ. The records arrive in pieces: monthly flight counts, monthly rain categories, and later the 2 × 3 table of seeded and unseeded storms against above-normal, normal and below-normal rain. We follow this one synthetic data stream through the whole construction and back to the decision (Studies 83–90, held-out seeds, every check pre-registered and frozen with SHA-256). The data give a credal fibre and its probability bands; the margins give toric chambers and walls; the margins also set the mirror potential of the degree-six del Pezzo surface, whose thimbles form an exceptional collection in its Fukaya–Seidel category. The experiment is a carrier for a realistic decision problem, not a claim about seeding. 1 What the example verifies. Each layer is tested on held-out data: (i) credal walls lie on the chamber walls, while Stokes events are mutations; (ii) margin-order ties are collision walls where two orthogonal objects swap, confirmed at the Floer level on 10 of 12 brackets (the other two, one not audited and one with a non-minimal representative, stay in the record); (iii) a full twist of the potential acts as the Serre functor; (iv) the support region of a vector-valued hypothesis is cut out by Markov moves on the table; (v) poisoning that preserves the

summary: Collecting data from wireless sensors can be challenging when limited communication infrastructure prevents them from offloading their measurements. In such settings, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can exploit their mobility to harvest data locally, while coordinated UAV teams can provide efficient and redundant coverage of remote areas. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables such teams to learn decentralized coordination policies. However, training separate policies for different team and sensor populations is costly, and fixed-population policies may be vulnerable to agent failures. This work proposes F-MADDPG, a flexible variant of Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) that supports data harvesting with varying numbers of wireless sensors and UAVs. The framework also accommodates unexpected catastrophic failures that permanently remove agents during a mission. We compare F-MADDPG with a MADDPG baseline that uses multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and evaluate training strategies based on team-size sampling and exposure to agent terminations. The results show that F-MADDPG learns across the evaluated population sizes, completes missions faster than the baseline on average, benefits from inverse-cardinality team-size sampling compared with uniform sampling, remains effective after permanent agent losses, and gains no consistent benefit from exposure to failures during training.
title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-UAV Data Harvesting Under Variable Team Sizes and Agent Loss

summary: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.

summary: As agents based on vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly interpret social-media content, errors in their analysis may lend credibility to rumors and amplify their spread. In this paper, we study the problem of visual cognitive collusion, in which coordinated posts combine authentic images and locally faithful captions to induce VLM agents to infer and accept attacker-chosen target claims through their own reasoning. To enable systematic evaluation of this cognitive threat, we introduce a new benchmark comprising 544 target cases and 33.2K candidate images across eight application domains. We further propose VisualMontage, a multi-agent framework for simulating such attacks through narrative planning, image selection and ordering, and caption assignment under iterative review. We evaluate this threat through extensive experiments across 12 vision-language models, examining modality effects, production-team components, and downstream defenses. Using identical attack feeds across models without victim-specific optimization, we demonstrate cross-model transferability, achieving mean attack success rates of 61.93% for proprietary models and 68.71% for open-weight models. Moreover, 92.65% of generated feeds pass independent model-based validity auditing. Even after downstream review, residual attack success rates range from 35.3% to 76.7% across the evaluated configurations. Our additional controlled comparisons further reveal that captions can improve model-rated posting naturalness while reducing attack success. Together, these findings reveal a novel cognitive threat in social-media interpretation and motivate safeguards that assess how authentic posts jointly shape agents' reasoning and conclusions.
title: VisualMontage: Manipulating the Beliefs of Vision-Language Agents with Authentic Image Sequences

summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to time series reasoning. However, current evaluations often give models events in chronological order and already matched to the time series. This makes it unclear whether models use timestamps to connect events with observations or simply take shortcuts. To expose this ambiguity, we reformulate time series reasoning from a world-to-series projection perspective, viewing timestamps as explicit indices that connect numerical observations and external events to shared world states. We identify three structures that timestamps can make explicit: temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment. Building on this perspective, we develop a diagnostic protocol that distinguishes timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts, a distinction that accuracy-based benchmarks cannot make. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that high accuracy can persist when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed, while breaking event-series alignment induces systematic failures. When context is pre-aligned, models barely need timestamps. When order is missing, they use dates to recall world knowledge. Without dates, they rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps. summary: Merchant underwriting becomes vulnerable when evidence is evaluated without enough visibility into its source, freshness, relationship to the applicant, or meaning for the proposed activity. Individually favorable checks do not necessarily establish that the same business is operating the merchant account, that its representative may bind it, or that its settlement instructions are authorized. We describe three failure modes of fragmented underwriting: distance from the source, the gap between a decision and the evidence needed to justify it; the correlation gap, in which material relationships among the person, legal entity, owners or controllers, representative, business activity, and settlement destination are not evaluated when each signal is considered alone; and point-in-time controls, in which a historical verification is treated as present eligibility. We map these failure modes to identity-proofing, customer-due-diligence, sanctions, third-party-risk, card-network, and Nacha requirements, and propose a merchant-underwriting application of the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture built on provenance, correlation, and persistence. The application keeps a logically unified evidence record that identifies what was checked, the subject and relationship involved, the relevant times, the applicable policy, the decision, and any exceptions, and it keeps evidence validation, applicant verification, organizational authority, and the institution's risk judgment separate. We also set out a proposed evidence and decision receipt, a defined 90-day shadow enrollment pilot with adjudicated outcome measures and deliberate control-failure tests, and a ten-question self-assessment. Proposed controls, illustrative scenarios, and pilot measures are identified as such and are not represented as observed production results.

We describe three failure modes of fragmented underwriting: distance from the source, the gap between a decision and the evidence needed to justify it; the correlation gap, in which material relationships among the person, legal entity, owners or controllers, representative, business activity, and settlement destination are not evaluated when each signal is considered alone; and point-in-time controls, in which a historical verification is treated as present eligibility. We map these failure modes to identity-proofing, customer-due-diligence, sanctions, third-party-risk, card-network, and Nacha requirements, and propose a merchant-underwriting application of the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture built on provenance, correlation, and persistence. The application keeps a logically unified evidence record that identifies what was checked, the subject and relationship involved, the relevant times, the applicable policy, the decision, and any exceptions, and it keeps evidence validation, applicant verification, organizational authority, and the institution's risk judgment separate. We also set out a proposed evidence and decision receipt, a defined 90-day shadow enrollment pilot with adjudicated outcome measures and deliberate control-failure tests, and a ten-question self-assessment. Proposed controls, illustrative scenarios, and pilot measures are identified as such and are not represented as observed production results.

summary: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.
title: HoMe: Toward Practical Harness Optimization of Memory Systems for AI Assistants

summary: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.
title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models

summary: Failure analyses of monocular depth models often name a cause for each error, such as an occluding boundary, a thin object or a reflective surface, but such labels are rarely tested. We present the Vision Error Observatory (VEO), an audit that finds regions failing the $δ_1$ criterion on sensor-measured pixels, labels each with a likely cause or abstains, and then subjects the labels to four tests: agreement with object annotations on data the label model never saw, agreement with blinded human raters, response to targeted image edits, and value as a training signal. We apply it to eight models on NYU Depth V2, DIODE and iBims-1, with labels also checked on Hypersim, and fix most decision rules before their results. The occluding-boundary label agrees with annotations (AUROC 0.85 on NYU, 0.81 on Hypersim, 0.69 on iBims-1), but a single depth-edge cue does as well, and most boundary failures of the strongest model vanish under a 2-pixel tolerance. The reflection label does not transfer to synthetic data, the textureless label is near chance against annotations, and only one of four edit tests, an exploratory one, supports its label. Evaluated against five blinded raters, VEO's labels matched the human consensus only at chance level (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.05). In addition, an increase in the weight on the diagnosed regions during fine-tuning led to an increase in the error on targeted pixels at every weight tested. The architecture-specific failure fingerprint claimed by an earlier version of this project also failed to replicate across the datasets. Plausible failure explanations, in short, need to be tested before they are trusted; we release the protocol, code, ratings and every result file.
title: Plausible Is Not Proven: Testing Failure Explanations in Monocular Depth Estimation

summary: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers

summary: Background. Renal fibrosis accompanies progression in many forms of chronic kidney disease. In adults with arterial hypertension, measures of fibrosis, routine kidney tests and prediction of kidney failure address different clinical questions. Methods. This narrative review used targeted PubMed searches for studies of hypertensive kidney disease, biopsy-defined fibrosis, urinary Dickkopf-3, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and kidney failure prediction. Primary studies and nephrology guidance were selected according to relevance to clinical assessment and interpreted with attention to population and outcome. Results. Severe interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy was associated with a 3.42-fold hazard of progression relative to minimal scarring in a mixed native kidney biopsy cohort after adjustment for clinical variables. Elevated urinary Dickkopf-3 was associated with short-term loss of estimated filtration in a mixed chronic kidney disease population. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging correlated with histologic fibrosis in a cross-sectional biopsy study. These observations support further validation in adults with hypertension. Serial estimated glomerular filtration rate and urine albumin measurements remain the basis of clinical risk assessment. In established moderate-to-advanced chronic kidney disease, an externally validated kidney failure equation provides an appropriate benchmark for determining whether fibrosis measures and inherited risk indicators add prognostic information.
tags: albuminuria, arterial hypertension, chronic kidney disease, kidney failure risk, renal fibrosis, urinary Dickkopf-3.

summary: Esta pieza falla una sola pregunta: qué densidad de colmenas por hectárea recomendar para el aguacate Hass en Colombia, contando solo lo que un ensayo con densidades comparadas sostenga. La respuesta es estrecha y es colombiana: el único ensayo localizado que compara densidades de Apis mellifera en Hass midiendo cosecha es el de Popayán, Cauca (Peña Mojica, 2017; Peña y Carabalí, 2018), y sostiene 4 y 6 colmenas por hectárea —con colonias Langstroth de diez marcos, cinco poblados con abejas adultas y tres con cría, reina joven— frente a no instalar colmenas: 38,2 y 46,2 kg de fruto por árbol contra 21,6 kg del testigo, en huertos de seis años sembrados a 6 × 6 m. Dentro del ensayo, 6 rindió más que 4 en kilos por árbol; en número de frutos, 4 y 6 no se distinguieron. Ninguna densidad mayor de 6 tiene, en lo leído, un ensayo de rendimiento en Hass que la sostenga: el óptimo es un hueco impreso, y las cifras de manual que circulan por encima (8 en Israel, 4–10 en Nueva Zelanda, hasta 24 en un ensayo español que midió deposición de polen y no rendimiento) no son mediciones de cosecha. La recomendación que circula en Colombia —dos colmenas por hectárea, de experto en prensa, sin ensayo citado— queda por debajo de la menor densidad con respuesta medida. El dinero se convierte solo desde el Δ de rendimiento del ensayo: a la densidad de siembra del propio ensayo (278 árboles/ha), el paso de 0 a 6 colmenas/ha son 6.833 kg/ha adicionales, que a precios mayoristas SIPSA de noviembre de 2026 valen en bruto $31,7 millones por hectárea en el escenario bajo y $46,5 millones en el alto (CALCULADO); el costo incremental completo no se puede cerrar, porque el único precio de alquiler fechado localizado es el del propio ensayo ($40.000 por colmena por mes, 2015) y el precio vigente no se verificó: el neto es un hueco impreso junto a la cifra. Cotas de transferencia: el ensayo asignó un solo huerto a cada densidad —la densidad quedó confundida con el huerto—, midió una sola cosecha en árboles jóvenes de Popayán (1.735 m s. n. m.), sin cultivar polinizador tipo B declarado y con abejas del ambiente ya presentes en el testigo (2,72 abejas por árbol y minuto sin instalar una sola colmena). La densidad recomendada viaja, por tanto, atada a la fuerza de colonia del ensayo y a huertos parecidos a los del ensayo; fuera de ahí, lo transferible es el método de verificación —contar abejas por árbol durante la fase femenina— y no la promesa del mismo Δ.
title: Aguacate Hass: la densidad de colmenas con ensayo, y el hueco del óptimo

Ninguna densidad mayor de 6 tiene, en lo leído, un ensayo de rendimiento en Hass que la sostenga: el óptimo es un hueco impreso, y las cifras de manual que circulan por encima (8 en Israel, 4–10 en Nueva Zelanda, hasta 24 en un ensayo español que midió deposición de polen y no rendimiento) no son mediciones de cosecha. La recomendación que circula en Colombia —dos colmenas por hectárea, de experto en prensa, sin ensayo citado— queda por debajo de la menor densidad con respuesta medida. El dinero se convierte solo desde el Δ de rendimiento del ensayo: a la densidad de siembra del propio ensayo (278 árboles/ha), el paso de 0 a 6 colmenas/ha son 6.833 kg/ha adicionales, que a precios mayoristas SIPSA de noviembre de 2026 valen en bruto $31,7 millones por hectárea en el escenario bajo y $46,5 millones en el alto (CALCULADO); el costo incremental completo no se puede cerrar, porque el único precio de alquiler fechado localizado es el del propio ensayo ($40.000 por colmena por mes, 2015) y el precio vigente no se verificó: el neto es un hueco impreso junto a la cifra. Cotas de transferencia: el ensayo asignó un solo huerto a cada densidad —la densidad quedó confundida con el huerto—, midió una sola cosecha en árboles jóvenes de Popayán (1.735 m s. n. m.), sin cultivar polinizador tipo B declarado y con abejas del ambiente ya presentes en el testigo (2,72 abejas por árbol y minuto sin instalar una sola colmena). La densidad recomendada viaja, por tanto, atada a la fuerza de colonia del ensayo y a huertos parecidos a los del ensayo; fuera de ahí, lo transferible es el método de verificación —contar abejas por árbol durante la fase femenina— y no la promesa del mismo Δ.

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Flip some fair coins and give each a real weight, with squared weights adding to one. summary: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

summary: Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model's own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM's success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.
title: Long-Horizon Planning with Latent World Models via Graph Anchors

summary: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.
title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies

summary: Accurate and early classification of brain tumours from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for treatment planning, yet many published deep learning studies are trained and tested on small, single-source datasets, reporting accuracies that may not hold outside these datasets. This study compares six deep learning architectures for four-class classification (healthy, meningioma, glioma and pituitary tumour): a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN), an attention-based CNN, ShuffleNet, and EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50 and Xception augmented with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). The models were trained on a corpus assembled from four publicly available MRI datasets. Because these datasets carry no patient identifiers, a leakage-aware pipeline was developed that removes exact duplicates using MD5 hashing (550 images) and near-duplicates using perceptual hashing (8,024 images), and assigns visually similar images to the same fold during 5-fold group cross-validation. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) test on a fully held-out dataset was used to measure cross-dataset generalisation. Under a conventional random split, ShuffleNet achieved 97.1% accuracy with 1.2M parameters. Under leakage-aware group K-fold cross-validation, ShuffleNetV2 (98.41%) and EfficientNet-B0 (98.23%) were statistically indistinguishable (paired t-test, p = 0.19), and both significantly outperformed the custom CNNs. On the held-out dataset, accuracy dropped for every model: EfficientNet-B0 generalised best (78.4%), while ShuffleNetV2 fell to 66.2%. Glioma-meningioma confusion was the dominant error mode, and Grad-CAM maps showed that predictions were driven by tumour regions. These results indicate that in-distribution accuracy alone overstates real-world performance and that leakage-aware and cross-dataset evaluation should be reported alongside it.

summary: In a Houston 2024 replay, replacing a fixed 20 percent battery reserve with a county-risk threshold raises observed five-hour backup coverage from 75.0 percent to 86.5 percent and adds USD 10.2 in modeled annualized margin per home (paired 95 percent interval: USD +1.7 to USD +21.7). The paired coverage-gain interval includes zero. This is a conditional simulation result, not measured company reliability. Residential batteries face this tradeoff because market discharge consumes energy also needed for household outages. We release HomeFleet-ERCOT, combining observed prices and county outages with identified simulated homes and causal controller inputs. We compare independent-home optimization with 21 proximal policy optimization (PPO) training runs; ten promise-cost candidates span 31.1 percent-96.3 percent backup coverage. Of these, 10 have lower modeled margin than fixed 20 percent, and 3 also have lower coverage. Chronological, geographic, fleet, and storm tests examine transfer. An alert charging override has a conditional energy-and-power sufficiency guarantee, but only 19.5 percent of 41 county mass-outage episodes provide enough continuous warning for every battery preset. Synthetic tests include short, missed, and false warnings, load uplift, capacity loss, and dropout. A static AC audit retains existing feeder violations; aging comparisons expose model sensitivity. The released benchmark, controllers, and checkpoints provide a reproducible basis for comparing these tradeoffs. This work supports the design of residential battery programs that assess market value and household backup service together.
title: Adaptive Reliability Reserves for Residential Battery Fleets
